Newsom’s poison-pill problem
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones)
10/26/2026 09:00 AM EDT
California Gov. Gavin Newsom attends a rally with members of the state's Democratic Party, organized labor, and other advocates in San Francisco, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. | Heather Diehl/AP
DOUBLE TROUBLE — If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to Gavin Newsom . But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder Sergey Brin and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible. One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%. And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
Newsom, a likely presidential contender, already has taken considerable political heat (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/11/billionaire-tax-gavin-newsom-01070600) for his opposition to Prop 40, which he says would devastate California’s finances (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/12/newsom-unloads-on-california-wealth-tax-proposal-00723732) by pushing wealthy taxpayers out of the state. And if Prop 42 ends up blocking the tax over the will of the voters, it would only give more fuel to critics accusing the governor of carrying the billionaires’ water.
Rep. Ro Khanna has hammered that point as he and Newsom circle each other ahead of a potential presidential matchup. Khanna has leaned into the wealth tax as a way to both bolster his progressive bona fides and differentiate himself from Newsom, and he has excoriated Newsom for backing Prop 42.
“If a majority of Californians vote yes on Prop 40, that’s a mandate to make billionaires pay their fair share,” Khanna said in a statement to Playbook. “Overturning that through the billionaire-funded loophole that Governor Newsom is championing would be a betrayal of the voters who fought for this. The Democratic Party has to decide whether it stands with working people or with the donor class. I know which side I’m on.”
Advertisements for Prop 42 do not directly link the proposal to the billionaires tax. Proponents are instead emphasizing the other main component of the measure: a prohibition on new taxes on financial assets such as stocks and retirement accounts.
“Californians should never have to worry that politicians will come after the retirement savings they spent a lifetime earning. Yet five proposals in recent years show that the threat is real,” said Brian Marvel , president of the law enforcement union Peace Officer Resource Association of California, which has endorsed the initiative. “Prop 40 is just the latest example of this emerging threat. …Whatever happens with Prop 40, Prop 42 gives Californians the long-term protection they deserve.”
But to Prop 40 backers, Prop 42 is inextricable from the efforts to quash the billionaire tax. The fact that deep-pocketed opponents funding the anti-Prop 40 campaign have spent nearly $40 million on advertising for a second measure that could kill the tax illustrates the lengths they are willing to go — and the resources they have at hand. (The same group behind Prop 42 also qualified a second measure, Proposition 41, which has been largely abandoned.)
Newsom did not elaborate on his reasons for backing Prop 42 when he rolled out his endorsements this month, but people close to him say his position is an extension of his long-standing opposition to a state-level wealth tax.
Some members of Newsom’s orbit acknowledge the potential of both measures passing could be politically explosive, but said it’s not a particularly pressing concern, mainly because they are increasingly certain the billionaires tax will fail. Private polling from three separate polling firms — FM3, Public Opinion Strategies and Binder Research — have consistently shown the measure hovering in the high 30s or low 40s, well short of the majority it would need to pass.
That is a notable divergence from public polls, which have regularly shown Prop 40 with a slight edge, usually with a plurality that falls short of 50%. That is a precarious place for a ballot measure (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) in the closing weeks of an election, but a more optimistic view than the opponents’ internals.
If the measure does pass, the political blast radius could be vast. It would be a jolt to the Democratic political establishment — including gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and powerful interest groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood — which led its imprimatur to the ‘no’ side. It would put billionaires like Brin and other ‘no on 40’ funders on notice that populist fury at growing wealth inequality is strong enough to overcome a deluge of political spending.
And for Newsom, it would put him on a losing side of the issue, even as he has called for raising taxes on billionaires on a national level (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/26/newsom-calls-for-national-billionaires-tax-00977751) and has struck other populist notes, including backing public equity stakes in the profits generated by artificial intelligence companies.
SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez blasted Newsom for abetting what she called a cynical scheme to disenfranchise millions of voters, calling Prop 42 a “misleading and dangerous threat to Californians.”
“Governor Newsom is in lockstep with his billionaire-backers,” Jimenez said in a statement. “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors: he’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask 200 billionaires to finally pay their fair share.”

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (left), and Randy Villegas, Democratic candidate for congress in California's 22nd District, wave at the end of a campaign rally on Oct. 23, 2026, in Bakersfield, California. | Jae C. Hong/AP
CLASS FOCUS — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made no mention of Prop 40 or the measures meant to undercut it as she rallied for progressive House candidate Randy Villegas in Bakersfield on Friday.
She didn’t spend much time discussing her and Villegas’ similar ideological profiles, either. Newsom’s poison-pill problem
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones)
10/26/2026 09:00 AM EDT
California Gov. Gavin Newsom attends a rally with members of the state's Democratic Party, organized labor, and other advocates in San Francisco, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. | Heather Diehl/AP
DOUBLE TROUBLE — If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to Gavin Newsom . But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder Sergey Brin and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible. One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%. And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
Newsom, a likely presidential contender, already has taken considerable political heat (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/11/billionaire-tax-gavin-newsom-01070600) for his opposition to Prop 40, which he says would devastate California’s finances (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/12/newsom-unloads-on-california-wealth-tax-proposal-00723732) by pushing wealthy taxpayers out of the state. And if Prop 42 ends up blocking the tax over the will of the voters, it would only give more fuel to critics accusing the governor of carrying the billionaires’ water.
Rep. Ro Khanna has hammered that point as he and Newsom circle each other ahead of a potential presidential matchup. Khanna has leaned into the wealth tax as a way to both bolster his progressive bona fides and differentiate himself from Newsom, and he has excoriated Newsom for backing Prop 42.
“If a majority of Californians vote yes on Prop 40, that’s a mandate to make billionaires pay their fair share,” Khanna said in a statement to Playbook. “Overturning that through the billionaire-funded loophole that Governor Newsom is championing would be a betrayal of the voters who fought for this. The Democratic Party has to decide whether it stands with working people or with the donor class. I know which side I’m on.”
Advertisements for Prop 42 do not directly link the proposal to the billionaires tax. Proponents are instead emphasizing the other main component of the measure: a prohibition on new taxes on financial assets such as stocks and retirement accounts.
“Californians should never have to worry that politicians will come after the retirement savings they spent a lifetime earning. Yet five proposals in recent years show that the threat is real,” said Brian Marvel , president of the law enforcement union Peace Officer Resource Association of California, which has endorsed the initiative. “Prop 40 is just the latest example of this emerging threat. …Whatever happens with Prop 40, Prop 42 gives Californians the long-term protection they deserve.”
But to Prop 40 backers, Prop 42 is inextricable from the efforts to quash the billionaire tax. The fact that deep-pocketed opponents funding the anti-Prop 40 campaign have spent nearly $40 million on advertising for a second measure that could kill the tax illustrates the lengths they are willing to go — and the resources they have at hand. (The same group behind Prop 42 also qualified a second measure, Proposition 41, which has been largely abandoned.)
Newsom did not elaborate on his reasons for backing Prop 42 when he rolled out his endorsements this month, but people close to him say his position is an extension of his long-standing opposition to a state-level wealth tax.
Some members of Newsom’s orbit acknowledge the potential of both measures passing could be politically explosive, but said it’s not a particularly pressing concern, mainly because they are increasingly certain the billionaires tax will fail. Private polling from three separate polling firms — FM3, Public Opinion Strategies and Binder Research — have consistently shown the measure hovering in the high 30s or low 40s, well short of the majority it would need to pass.
That is a notable divergence from public polls, which have regularly shown Prop 40 with a slight edge, usually with a plurality that falls short of 50%. That is a precarious place for a ballot measure (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) in the closing weeks of an election, but a more optimistic view than the opponents’ internals.
If the measure does pass, the political blast radius could be vast. It would be a jolt to the Democratic political establishment — including gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and powerful interest groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood — which led its imprimatur to the ‘no’ side. It would put billionaires like Brin and other ‘no on 40’ funders on notice that populist fury at growing wealth inequality is strong enough to overcome a deluge of political spending.
And for Newsom, it would put him on a losing side of the issue, even as he has called for raising taxes on billionaires on a national level (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/26/newsom-calls-for-national-billionaires-tax-00977751) and has struck other populist notes, including backing public equity stakes in the profits generated by artificial intelligence companies.
SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez blasted Newsom for abetting what she called a cynical scheme to disenfranchise millions of voters, calling Prop 42 a “misleading and dangerous threat to Californians.”
“Governor Newsom is in lockstep with his billionaire-backers,” Jimenez said in a statement. “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors: he’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask 200 billionaires to finally pay their fair share.”

You earned and saved it.
Now WE need to protect it.
Californians already pay income taxes on the money they earn.
Politicians shouldn’t be able to tax it again when it’s sitting in our retirement and savings accounts.
Prop 42 (2026) prevents double taxation by closing a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows politicians and special interests to tax retirement accounts, life savings, and other personal property.
After a lifetime of hard work, Californians deserve the peace of mind of knowing the money you’ve earned and saved will be there when you need it.

Billionaires Flood Final Stretch with $50M to Sink Prop. 40, California’s Wealth Tax
A billionaire-backed group fighting Proposition 40 spent more than $50 million over the past week on efforts to thwart the wealth tax.
By Ben Paviour
The Sacramento Bee
(TNS)
A billionaire-backed group fighting Proposition 40 spent more than $50 million over the past week on efforts to thwart the wealth tax—a surge that suggests the tax’s critics aren’t taking favorable polling as a sure sign (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) of Election Day success.
Put more simply, the group, Building a Better California, spent far more in a week than the $32.7 million the primary Prop. 40 campaign committee raised in 10 months.
“We are sprinting, not strolling, through the finish line,” said Evan Westrup, a spokesperson for the No on 40 campaign.
Public polling suggests the tax’s critics have the wind at their back. A Public Policy Institute of California survey released Tuesday (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) showed 46% of likely voters support the proposed wealth tax, down from 52% in September. Prop. 42, a measure designed to prevent future personal property taxes that would also block the billionaire tax if it wins more votes, polled better, winning 51% support.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the union sponsoring the one-time, 5% tax, says it will raise $100 billion to address federal healthcare cuts caused by H.R. 1, a tax cut and Medicaid overhaul bill signed by President Donald Trump last year.
Critics of the tax include not just billionaires and business groups but Democratic politicians like Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Sacramento Mayor Darrell Steinberg as well as some left-leaning groups like Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California. Opponents argue the tax will chase billionaires out of the state, endangering the state’s economy and future tax collections.
In a statement, SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez said the late anti-billionaire tax spending was “as obscene as it is revealing.”
“Sen. Bernie Sanders put it plainly: These billionaires would rather see poor children die of cancer than pay a little more in taxes,” Jimenez said, referring to the Vermont independent who is the tax’s highest-profile supporter. “That is a profoundly troubling indictment of their priorities—and raises serious questions about the influence of extraordinary wealth on our democracy.”

Democratic consultant Steve Maviglio, who is not involved in the fight, said the spending showed the tax’s critics “don’t just want to win, they want to win big.”
“They want to send a message: don’t mess with us,” Maviglio said. “They might have seen something in their polling—hard to tell—but when you have it, you spend it.”
A fundraising blitz
Raising money has not been an issue for critics of the one-time, 5% wealth tax.
Building a Better California has been on a fall fundraising spree, drawing more than $58 million in the first 17 days of October and $164 million since the beginning of September.
At least 15 of the 53 donors who gave money this month had no history of state-level political contributions, and many more hadn’t cut checks in at least a decade. The donors span longtime Democratic backers like billionaire investor John Pritzker to first-time donors like investor Jack Altman, brother of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who has given $102 million in the group, requested reinforcements from a broader group of donors to help spike the tax, according to a source familiar with anti-Prop. 40 efforts who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The source said the group would endure beyond the wealth tax fight, although it remained to be seen how it would be structured and what issues it would prioritize. A Building a Better California representative said the group would focus on affordability, the economy and quality-of-life issues for Californians.
Democratic consultant Eric Jaye, who has worked with some tech leaders, said the fight over the redistribution of wealth was certain to outlast the battle over Prop. 40, which had “activated the richest people on the planet.”
Jaye argued the late spending was intended to “run up the score” to discourage future taxation efforts from SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan, a mission he said was unlikely to succeed given Regan’s love of ballot wars and populist anti-billionaire sentiment among voters.
“The billionaires are going to win this battle, but this war is just starting,” Jaye said.

Billionaires Flood Final Stretch with $50M to Sink Prop. 40, California’s Wealth Tax
A billionaire-backed group fighting Proposition 40 spent more than $50 million over the past week on efforts to thwart the wealth tax.
By Ben Paviour
The Sacramento Bee
(TNS)
A billionaire-backed group fighting Proposition 40 spent more than $50 million over the past week on efforts to thwart the wealth tax—a surge that suggests the tax’s critics aren’t taking favorable polling as a sure sign (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) of Election Day success.
Put more simply, the group, Building a Better California, spent far more in a week than the $32.7 million the primary Prop. 40 campaign committee raised in 10 months.
“We are sprinting, not strolling, through the finish line,” said Evan Westrup, a spokesperson for the No on 40 campaign.
Public polling suggests the tax’s critics have the wind at their back. A Public Policy Institute of California survey released Tuesday (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) showed 46% of likely voters support the proposed wealth tax, down from 52% in September. Prop. 42, a measure designed to prevent future personal property taxes that would also block the billionaire tax if it wins more votes, polled better, winning 51% support.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the union sponsoring the one-time, 5% tax, says it will raise $100 billion to address federal healthcare cuts caused by H.R. 1, a tax cut and Medicaid overhaul bill signed by President Donald Trump last year.
Critics of the tax include not just billionaires and business groups but Democratic politicians like Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Sacramento Mayor Darrell Steinberg as well as some left-leaning groups like Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California. Opponents argue the tax will chase billionaires out of the state, endangering the state’s economy and future tax collections.
In a statement, SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez said the late anti-billionaire tax spending was “as obscene as it is revealing.”
“Sen. Bernie Sanders put it plainly: These billionaires would rather see poor children die of cancer than pay a little more in taxes,” Jimenez said, referring to the Vermont independent who is the tax’s highest-profile supporter. “That is a profoundly troubling indictment of their priorities—and raises serious questions about the influence of extraordinary wealth on our democracy.”

Democratic consultant Steve Maviglio, who is not involved in the fight, said the spending showed the tax’s critics “don’t just want to win, they want to win big.”
“They want to send a message: don’t mess with us,” Maviglio said. “They might have seen something in their polling—hard to tell—but when you have it, you spend it.”
A fundraising blitz
Raising money has not been an issue for critics of the one-time, 5% wealth tax.
Building a Better California has been on a fall fundraising spree, drawing more than $58 million in the first 17 days of October and $164 million since the beginning of September.
At least 15 of the 53 donors who gave money this month had no history of state-level political contributions, and many more hadn’t cut checks in at least a decade. The donors span longtime Democratic backers like billionaire investor John Pritzker to first-time donors like investor Jack Altman, brother of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who has given $102 million in the group, requested reinforcements from a broader group of donors to help spike the tax, according to a source familiar with anti-Prop. 40 efforts who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The source said the group would endure beyond the wealth tax fight, although it remained to be seen how it would be structured and what issues it would prioritize. A Building a Better California representative said the group would focus on affordability, the economy and quality-of-life issues for Californians.
Democratic consultant Eric Jaye, who has worked with some tech leaders, said the fight over the redistribution of wealth was certain to outlast the battle over Prop. 40, which had “activated the richest people on the planet.”
Jaye argued the late spending was intended to “run up the score” to discourage future taxation efforts from SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan, a mission he said was unlikely to succeed given Regan’s love of ballot wars and populist anti-billionaire sentiment among voters.
“The billionaires are going to win this battle, but this war is just starting,” Jaye said.

IGS was created a century ago to provide research expertise to the Legislature regarding public issues of the day. The Berkeley IGS Poll is a periodic survey of California public opinion on important matters of politics, public policy, and public issues. The poll, which is disseminated widely, seeks to provide a broad measure of contemporary public opinion, and to generate data for subsequent scholarly analysis.
IGS Poll media releases and tabulations (2015 - current) can be downloaded from the eScholarship Repository of the California Digital Library (https://escholarship.org/uc/igs_poll).

Newsom’s poison-pill problem
By MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason), JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white) and BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones)
10/26/2026 09:00 AM EDT
California Gov. Gavin Newsom attends a rally with members of the state's Democratic Party, organized labor, and other advocates in San Francisco, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. | Heather Diehl/AP
DOUBLE TROUBLE — If voters approve Proposition 40’s tax on billionaires, it would be a rebuke to Gavin Newsom . But there’s an even worse scenario for the governor: the billionaire-backed Proposition 42 also passes, winning enough votes to wipe out the tax.
Prop 42 — funded by wealth tax opponents like Google co-founder Sergey Brin and endorsed by Newsom — contains a poison pill provision that would void Prop 40’s one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets. If both measures pass, whichever receives the most yes votes goes into effect.
That’s not the likeliest outcome, but also not impossible. One recent PPIC poll shows Prop 42 passing with 54% of the vote, and Prop 40 eking by with 52%. And it’s not hard to imagine the far-reaching uproar if voters approve a billionaires tax, only to be overruled by a billionaire-backed measure pitched as a protection for retirement savings.
Newsom, a likely presidential contender, already has taken considerable political heat (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/11/billionaire-tax-gavin-newsom-01070600) for his opposition to Prop 40, which he says would devastate California’s finances (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/01/12/newsom-unloads-on-california-wealth-tax-proposal-00723732) by pushing wealthy taxpayers out of the state. And if Prop 42 ends up blocking the tax over the will of the voters, it would only give more fuel to critics accusing the governor of carrying the billionaires’ water.
Rep. Ro Khanna has hammered that point as he and Newsom circle each other ahead of a potential presidential matchup. Khanna has leaned into the wealth tax as a way to both bolster his progressive bona fides and differentiate himself from Newsom, and he has excoriated Newsom for backing Prop 42.
“If a majority of Californians vote yes on Prop 40, that’s a mandate to make billionaires pay their fair share,” Khanna said in a statement to Playbook. “Overturning that through the billionaire-funded loophole that Governor Newsom is championing would be a betrayal of the voters who fought for this. The Democratic Party has to decide whether it stands with working people or with the donor class. I know which side I’m on.”
Advertisements for Prop 42 do not directly link the proposal to the billionaires tax. Proponents are instead emphasizing the other main component of the measure: a prohibition on new taxes on financial assets such as stocks and retirement accounts.
“Californians should never have to worry that politicians will come after the retirement savings they spent a lifetime earning. Yet five proposals in recent years show that the threat is real,” said Brian Marvel , president of the law enforcement union Peace Officer Resource Association of California, which has endorsed the initiative. “Prop 40 is just the latest example of this emerging threat. …Whatever happens with Prop 40, Prop 42 gives Californians the long-term protection they deserve.”
But to Prop 40 backers, Prop 42 is inextricable from the efforts to quash the billionaire tax. The fact that deep-pocketed opponents funding the anti-Prop 40 campaign have spent nearly $40 million on advertising for a second measure that could kill the tax illustrates the lengths they are willing to go — and the resources they have at hand. (The same group behind Prop 42 also qualified a second measure, Proposition 41, which has been largely abandoned.)
Newsom did not elaborate on his reasons for backing Prop 42 when he rolled out his endorsements this month, but people close to him say his position is an extension of his long-standing opposition to a state-level wealth tax.
Some members of Newsom’s orbit acknowledge the potential of both measures passing could be politically explosive, but said it’s not a particularly pressing concern, mainly because they are increasingly certain the billionaires tax will fail. Private polling from three separate polling firms — FM3, Public Opinion Strategies and Binder Research — have consistently shown the measure hovering in the high 30s or low 40s, well short of the majority it would need to pass.
That is a notable divergence from public polls, which have regularly shown Prop 40 with a slight edge, usually with a plurality that falls short of 50%. That is a precarious place for a ballot measure (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/15/california-wealth-tax-lagging-01119038) in the closing weeks of an election, but a more optimistic view than the opponents’ internals.
If the measure does pass, the political blast radius could be vast. It would be a jolt to the Democratic political establishment — including gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and powerful interest groups like the California Teachers Association and Planned Parenthood — which led its imprimatur to the ‘no’ side. It would put billionaires like Brin and other ‘no on 40’ funders on notice that populist fury at growing wealth inequality is strong enough to overcome a deluge of political spending.
And for Newsom, it would put him on a losing side of the issue, even as he has called for raising taxes on billionaires on a national level (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/06/26/newsom-calls-for-national-billionaires-tax-00977751) and has struck other populist notes, including backing public equity stakes in the profits generated by artificial intelligence companies.
SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez blasted Newsom for abetting what she called a cynical scheme to disenfranchise millions of voters, calling Prop 42 a “misleading and dangerous threat to Californians.”
“Governor Newsom is in lockstep with his billionaire-backers,” Jimenez said in a statement. “By voting yes on Prop 42, he’s showing California his true colors: he’d rather millions of children and families lose their healthcare than ask 200 billionaires to finally pay their fair share.”

CAMPAIGN YEAR
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (left), and Randy Villegas, Democratic candidate for congress in California's 22nd District, wave at the end of a campaign rally on Oct. 23, 2026, in Bakersfield, California. | Jae C. Hong/AP
CLASS FOCUS — Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez made no mention of Prop 40 or the measures meant to undercut it as she rallied for progressive House candidate Randy Villegas in Bakersfield on Friday.
She didn’t spend much time discussing her and Villegas’ similar ideological profiles, either. Instead, the potential presidential candidate, who has not endorsed the wealth tax, emphasized their working class origins, saying Villegas’ family’s story, immigrating from Mexico and starting an auto body shop, was the “American dream at work, where we start from nothing and we make something of ourselves.”
She compared his upbringing, working in the shop before becoming a political science professor, to hers, helping her mom clean houses growing up.

Villegas echoed the class-based appeals that have become foundational to their wing of the Democratic Party, while railing against Speaker Mike Johnson ’s recent visit to the Central Valley to campaign alongside his opponent, Rep. David Valadao . He urged attendees to tell their family members to vote, before joking: “Call your ex. Make sure they get their ballot in, but only if they’re going to vote for us, right?”

STAFF SPAT — The intra-party fight between Rep. Mike Thompson and challenger Eric Jones has spilled into a dispute between Thompson’s former staffers. The dust-up began when Jones released an ad (https://x.com/andrewsolender/status/2114083961836089529?s=46) featuring Thompson’s former communications director, T.J. Adams-Falconer , accusing the Democratic representative of being in office too long and part of a “corrupt political system.”
“Mike Thompson told me directly he plans to die in office,” Adams-Falconer says, before saying he’ll be voting for Jones. The ad shows a photo of Adams-Falconer standing next to the congressmember, along with other staff members.
The Thompson campaign responded with a letter from seven of those former staffers who take issue with Adams-Falconer’s assertion and are demanding the Jones campaign remove the image from the ad.
“Collectively, we have served Congressman Thompson for over thirty years, and none of us have ever heard the Congressman say anything of the kind,” the letter reads. “What we have heard him say is precisely the opposite — that he does NOT intend to die in office.”
Meanwhile, the Thompson campaign is hitting Jones for pouring more of his personal wealth into the contest. Jones loaned his campaign roughly $5 million this month, according to FEC filings, bringing his total investment in the race to nearly $15 million.
“Voters will not be deceived by a San Francisco venture capitalist air dropping into our communities to buy a seat in Congress,” Thomas Dowling , Thompson’s campaign manager, said in a statement.

WATERED DOWN — The center-left Majority Democrats, which represents younger Democratic officials, deleted a post criticizing Rep. Maxine Waters , 88, and the Capitol Hill “gerontocracy,” Jasper Goodman reports (https://www.politico.com/live-updates/2026/10/23/congress/democratic-group-walks-back-gerontocracy-swipe-against-maxine-waters-01134350). The deletion came after one of the group’s members, Rep. Ritchie Torres , pushed back against the post that appeared to take aim at Waters’ campaign to continue as the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee.
STARLINK SLOWDOWN — A trio of House Democrats representing Silicon Valley demanded that the White House investigate reports that SpaceX limited its military-grade version of Starlink satellite services to Ukrainians on the battlefield, writes Owen Dahlkamp (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/23/starshield-slowdown-probe-democrats-01133720).
In a letter to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles , Reps. Sam Liccardo , Jimmy Panetta and Khanna asked for a briefing within two weeks outlining who decided to restrict Starshield speeds, how they were implemented and if any contractual obligations were violated. The lawmakers also asked for details of whether similar vulnerabilities exist elsewhere.
The Wall Street Journal has reported (https://www.wsj.com/world/ukraine-starlink-elon-musk-trump-dbc49193) that Elon Musk ordered the slowdown of Starlink and that he spoke with President Donald Trump and other senior administration officials before the limits were imposed.

Adam Gray , and its slight Democratic voter registration edge, make it prime for a flip. Esparza is facing term-limited state Sen. Shannon Grove for the open seat, which is currently held by Republican Ted Gaines .

YES on Prop 42
Protect Your Retirement & Life Savings
Prop 42 is a measure on the November 3, 2026 ballot (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) , that protects Californians from double taxation on the money we earn by closing a loophole (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=) in California’s Constitution that allows new state taxes on retirement accounts, personal savings, pensions, and other personal property.
You earned and saved it.
Now WE need to protect it.
Californians already pay income taxes on the money they earn.
Politicians shouldn’t be able to tax it again when it’s sitting in our retirement and savings accounts.
Prop 42 (2026) prevents double taxation by closing a loophole in California’s Constitution that allows politicians and special interests to tax retirement accounts, life savings, and other personal property.
After a lifetime of hard work, Californians deserve the peace of mind of knowing the money you’ve earned and saved will be there when you need it.

Retirement Savings At Risk
California is now the third most expensive state to retire in the nation. (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__www.cnbc.com_make-2Dit_2025_01_19_most-2Dexpensive-2Dus-2Dstates-2Dto-2Dretire.html&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=q3QbdWzqFeD9B_wUx9JL86V-tLjHuGtDqGwUv2vctdw&e=) Every year, California’s high cost of living and high taxes make it harder for Californians to save. Millions work their entire lives to achieve retirement security.
You shouldn’t have to worry that the money you’ve worked hard to earn and save will be taxed twice.
Yet today, California’s Constitution does not protect retirement accounts, (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/42/arguments-rebuttals.htm) life savings, and other personal property from new state taxes—a loophole lawmakers and special interests have repeatedly tried to exploit.
You earned it. Prop 42 protects it.
You earned it.
Prop 42 protects it.

Prop 42 protects all personal property

What is Prop 42?
Prop 42 is a measure on California’s November 3, 2026 (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov_2026_general_pdf_prop42-2Dtext-2Dproposed-2Dlaws.pdf&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=c3Gqu-OMIDatgK3hnMmB3S2ODmqsGQ0poGtXleReCu8&e=) ballot that would prohibit new state taxes on personal property, including retirement accounts and savings, and ban retroactive state taxes (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=). (https://urldefense.proofpoint.com/v2/url?u=https-3A__voterguide.sos.ca.gov_propositions_42_&d=DwMGaQ&c=euGZstcaTDllvimEN8b7jXrwqOf-v5A_CdpgnVfiiMM&r=Lbak5eFZHnZSYhftzpqbORUrs1mHGbmgfEVBYVeetqU&m=3Kh86csSe4Cl6q9fcUvr1QX3IGpDHhcugmEJous0LV6L-5TYZP1t6L6mee4OHIHn&s=ufUF2OJehlbx--9fM7nvGFw4Qh_D0Cgtj_UKws5-HY0&e=)

Billionaires Flood Final Stretch with $50M to Sink Prop. 40, California’s Wealth Tax
A billionaire-backed group fighting Proposition 40 spent more than $50 million over the past week on efforts to thwart the wealth tax.
By Ben Paviour
The Sacramento Bee
(TNS)
A billionaire-backed group fighting Proposition 40 spent more than $50 million over the past week on efforts to thwart the wealth tax—a surge that suggests the tax’s critics aren’t taking favorable polling as a sure sign (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) of Election Day success.
Put more simply, the group, Building a Better California, spent far more in a week than the $32.7 million the primary Prop. 40 campaign committee raised in 10 months.
“We are sprinting, not strolling, through the finish line,” said Evan Westrup, a spokesperson for the No on 40 campaign.
Public polling suggests the tax’s critics have the wind at their back. A Public Policy Institute of California survey released Tuesday (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317804297.html) showed 46% of likely voters support the proposed wealth tax, down from 52% in September. Prop. 42, a measure designed to prevent future personal property taxes that would also block the billionaire tax if it wins more votes, polled better, winning 51% support.
SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the union sponsoring the one-time, 5% tax, says it will raise $100 billion to address federal healthcare cuts caused by H.R. 1, a tax cut and Medicaid overhaul bill signed by President Donald Trump last year.
Critics of the tax include not just billionaires and business groups but Democratic politicians like Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Sacramento Mayor Darrell Steinberg as well as some left-leaning groups like Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California. Opponents argue the tax will chase billionaires out of the state, endangering the state’s economy and future tax collections.
In a statement, SEIU-UHW chief of staff Suzanne Jimenez said the late anti-billionaire tax spending was “as obscene as it is revealing.”
“Sen. Bernie Sanders put it plainly: These billionaires would rather see poor children die of cancer than pay a little more in taxes,” Jimenez said, referring to the Vermont independent who is the tax’s highest-profile supporter. “That is a profoundly troubling indictment of their priorities—and raises serious questions about the influence of extraordinary wealth on our democracy.”

Democratic consultant Steve Maviglio, who is not involved in the fight, said the spending showed the tax’s critics “don’t just want to win, they want to win big.”
“They want to send a message: don’t mess with us,” Maviglio said. “They might have seen something in their polling—hard to tell—but when you have it, you spend it.”
A fundraising blitz
Raising money has not been an issue for critics of the one-time, 5% wealth tax.
Building a Better California has been on a fall fundraising spree, drawing more than $58 million in the first 17 days of October and $164 million since the beginning of September.
At least 15 of the 53 donors who gave money this month had no history of state-level political contributions, and many more hadn’t cut checks in at least a decade. The donors span longtime Democratic backers like billionaire investor John Pritzker to first-time donors like investor Jack Altman, brother of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.
Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who has given $102 million in the group, requested reinforcements from a broader group of donors to help spike the tax, according to a source familiar with anti-Prop. 40 efforts who was not authorized to speak publicly.
The source said the group would endure beyond the wealth tax fight, although it remained to be seen how it would be structured and what issues it would prioritize. A Building a Better California representative said the group would focus on affordability, the economy and quality-of-life issues for Californians.
Democratic consultant Eric Jaye, who has worked with some tech leaders, said the fight over the redistribution of wealth was certain to outlast the battle over Prop. 40, which had “activated the richest people on the planet.”
Jaye argued the late spending was intended to “run up the score” to discourage future taxation efforts from SEIU-UHW President Dave Regan, a mission he said was unlikely to succeed given Regan’s love of ballot wars and populist anti-billionaire sentiment among voters.
“The billionaires are going to win this battle, but this war is just starting,” Jaye said.

## Proposition 42 Would Reach Beyond Billionaires
Proposition 42 makes the fight broader.
It would prohibit new state taxes on personal property, including financial assets, and restrict retroactive taxes.
The measure would also invalidate certain taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, if they conflict with its provisions.
Supporters frame the proposal as protection for retirement savings, investments, and money people have already earned.
Its reach, however, extends well beyond a typical household’s retirement account.
It could also block future wealth taxes on business holdings, securities, and other assets.
The measure would therefore limit California’s ability to tax personal wealth, even in circumstances unrelated to the current billionaire dispute.
That broader reach explains why Proposition 42 has attracted fierce opposition from billionaire-tax supporters.
If Proposition 42 receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, the courts could find the measures conflict and prevent the wealth tax from taking effect.
In other words, voters aren’t merely deciding what happens to one proposed tax.
They’re also weighing how much room California should retain to create similar taxes later.

Neither side can guarantee its forecast.
Stock prices change, fortunes fluctuate, and tax rules influence financial decisions in ways that are difficult to predict.

Californians and Their GovernmentOctober 2026
Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.
If you have any questions or require additional information regarding this survey, please contact surveys@ppic.org

Full Crosstabs–Likely Voters Only
Methodology Note:
Findings are based on a survey of 1,728 California adult residents, conducted online using the Ipsos KnowledgePanel. Interviews were conducted in
English and Spanish according to the respondents’ preferences. The median time to complete the survey was 14 minutes. Interviewing took place
from October 16—22, 2026.
These crosstabs are based on a subgroup of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error, taking design effects from weighting into consideration, is ±3.8
percent at the 95 percent confidence level for the unweighted sample of 1,086 likely voters. The sampling error for unweighted likely voter subgroups
is larger. Sampling error is only one type of error to which surveys are subject. Results may also be affected by factors such as question wording,
question order, and survey timing.

## Proposition 42 Would Reach Beyond Billionaires
Proposition 42 makes the fight broader.
It would prohibit new state taxes on personal property, including financial assets, and restrict retroactive taxes.
The measure would also invalidate certain taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, if they conflict with its provisions.
Supporters frame the proposal as protection for retirement savings, investments, and money people have already earned.
Its reach, however, extends well beyond a typical household’s retirement account.
It could also block future wealth taxes on business holdings, securities, and other assets.
The measure would therefore limit California’s ability to tax personal wealth, even in circumstances unrelated to the current billionaire dispute.
That broader reach explains why Proposition 42 has attracted fierce opposition from billionaire-tax supporters.
If Proposition 42 receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, the courts could find the measures conflict and prevent the wealth tax from taking effect.
In other words, voters aren’t merely deciding what happens to one proposed tax.
They’re also weighing how much room California should retain to create similar taxes later.

Neither side can guarantee its forecast.
Stock prices change, fortunes fluctuate, and tax rules influence financial decisions in ways that are difficult to predict.

## Proposition 42 Would Reach Beyond Billionaires
Proposition 42 makes the fight broader.
It would prohibit new state taxes on personal property, including financial assets, and restrict retroactive taxes.
The measure would also invalidate certain taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, if they conflict with its provisions.
Supporters frame the proposal as protection for retirement savings, investments, and money people have already earned.
Its reach, however, extends well beyond a typical household’s retirement account.
It could also block future wealth taxes on business holdings, securities, and other assets.
The measure would therefore limit California’s ability to tax personal wealth, even in circumstances unrelated to the current billionaire dispute.
That broader reach explains why Proposition 42 has attracted fierce opposition from billionaire-tax supporters.
If Proposition 42 receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, the courts could find the measures conflict and prevent the wealth tax from taking effect.
In other words, voters aren’t merely deciding what happens to one proposed tax.
They’re also weighing how much room California should retain to create similar taxes later.

# Study examines potential impact of retirement taxes as Californians prepare to vote on Prop. 42
(FOX40.COM) — Supporters of Proposition 42 are speaking out ahead of the November election, pointing to a new economic study that warns a future California tax on retirement and other personal assets could significantly reduce retirement income and force some workers to delay retirement.
Commissioned by Prop.
42 backers, the study comes ahead of November’s election, when voters will decide on the measure proposing a prohibition of new state taxes on personal property, including retirement accounts and personal savings.
...
The study, conducted by Brad Williams, a former Chief Economist and Director of Budget Overview and Fiscal Forecasting at the Legislative Analyst’s Office, models how a 1% annual tax could affect workers with 401(k) accounts and public employees with pensions.

## Proposition 42 Would Reach Beyond Billionaires
Proposition 42 makes the fight broader.
It would prohibit new state taxes on personal property, including financial assets, and restrict retroactive taxes.
The measure would also invalidate certain taxes enacted after January 1, 2026, if they conflict with its provisions.
Supporters frame the proposal as protection for retirement savings, investments, and money people have already earned.
Its reach, however, extends well beyond a typical household’s retirement account.
It could also block future wealth taxes on business holdings, securities, and other assets.
The measure would therefore limit California’s ability to tax personal wealth, even in circumstances unrelated to the current billionaire dispute.
That broader reach explains why Proposition 42 has attracted fierce opposition from billionaire-tax supporters.
If Proposition 42 receives more yes votes than Proposition 40, the courts could find the measures conflict and prevent the wealth tax from taking effect.
In other words, voters aren’t merely deciding what happens to one proposed tax.
They’re also weighing how much room California should retain to create similar taxes later.

How this is built
Proposition 42 is forecast as a property tax measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . Comparable measures from 2018 to 2024 set how far its Yes share moves with California 's partisanship, and each county moves with its own age, education, race and density mix as well as its 2024 presidential vote, so no two counties share a margin by default. How it reached the ballot moves it further. Polls then pull the forecast toward them by recency and size, after splitting undecided voters two to one for No. Sources: elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ccrov/2026/june/26179jj.pdf), growsf.org (https://growsf.org/news/2026-07-02-14-state-measures/), ppic.org (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), escholarship.org (https://escholarship.org/content/qt3w14s99c/qt3w14s99c.pdf). Director, Berkeley IGS Poll 
In a poll of California voters completed a little more than one week before Tuesday’s midterm elections, the Berkeley IGS Poll finds voters moving to the No side on Proposition 40 to impose a one-time tax on taxpayers with assets over $1 billion.
The poll finds 50% of likely voters now intending to vote No on the initiative, while 42% are voting Yes.
The 8 percentage-point No side advantage in the current poll represents a significant change from two earlier IGS Polls completed in August and
September in which the Yes side held narrow leads.

How this is built
Proposition 42 is forecast as a property tax measure whose Yes vote leans Republican . #### Proposition 43
Proposition 43 combined two hot topics of taxes and voting.
If approved, it would amend the state constitution to make it harder to raise local special taxes.
Citizen initiatives asking voters to approve local special taxes would require a two-thirds vote instead of a simple majority to be enacted.

***Ownership of Financial Assets Is Not Taxed.*** The ownership of many types of personal property is not taxed.

Although the state does tax income people make from their financial assets, there is no tax for simply owning those assets.
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.

This could reduce future tax revenues.

# Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
#### Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters.
...
### Fiscal Effect
***Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future.*** Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future.
This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.
This could reduce future tax revenues.
When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

# Proposition 42
Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Prohibits New Taxes on Financial Assets or Other Personal Property.*** Under Proposition 42, new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property would not be allowed.
***Limits Retroactive Taxes.*** Proposition 42 limits the situations that a ballot measure or the Legislature can raise any tax retroactively.
A retroactive tax is one that applies to things that happened in the past.
An example is a tax on money someone earned two years ago.
#### Potential Interactions With Other Propositions
If Proposition 42 receives more “yes” votes than Proposition 40 on this same ballot, then Proposition 40 could be stopped from becoming law even if it gets yes votes from a majority of voters.
...
### Fiscal Effect
***Possibility That Tax Revenues Will Be Lower in the Future.*** Proposition 42 restricts the options the state has to raise taxes in the future.
This could make it somewhat harder for the state to raise taxes.
This could reduce future tax revenues.
When and by how much future revenues would be reduced is unclear.
## Yes/No Statement
A **YES** vote on this measure means: The state could not establish new taxes on the ownership of financial assets or other personal property.

The measure, put forth by a health workers union to plug holes in the state Medicaid and education budgets created by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, immediately raised the hackles of California’s three-comma club, whose members tend to be allergic to taxation.
The claim that losing 250 billionaires would kill the state tax base and stifle innovation is laughable. They pay minimal taxes, and there are tens of thousands of Californians worth $30 million and up.
These moguls, led by Google co-founder Sergey Brin (who now claims residence in Nevada), started a group called Building a Better California (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/), which they’ve bankrolled to the tune of $333 million—about 0.1 percent of the combined net worth of its top 5 backers (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/technology/proposition-40-california-billionaire-tax.html): Brin, Google’s Steve Schmidt, venture capitalist John Doerr, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, and investor Vinod Khosla. The group has blanketed the state political landscape with anti-Prop 40 advertising and propaganda. It also bankrolled two poison pill initiatives, Props. 41 and 42, that we’ll talk about in a minute.
There are legitimate critiques of Prop. 40: Voter initiatives are a lousy way to do tax policy. Maybe it won’t bring in as much cash as projected. It’ll be challenged in court. (What isn’t?) Voters might conflate it with another measure, Prop. 3, that would extend an existing tax on income in excess of $371,000 ($742,000 for joint filers) to fund public education.
One big (valid) gripe about Prop. 40 is that it’s one-and-done. The California Teachers Union, for instance, says it opposes the measure on the grounds that it “will not provide the sustainable and long-lasting funding that our schools and communities deserve.” Such arguments are politically safe for Democratic politicians such as Xavier Becerra—who will almost certainly replace Gavin Newsom as governor, and who opposes Prop. 40 (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/2026/07/31/becerra-announces-positions-on-key-november-ballot-measures/) (though, in true weasel fashion, he has declined to take a position on the competing propositions, 41 and 42). The fact that most of the Prop. 40 revenues are earmarked for health care also may have miffed some of the other unions that oppose it (https://www.wsj.com/politics/california-billionaire-tax-democratic-party-f4729c1d?st=99MAWA&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink), and that would prefer some of the money go toward their own interests.
But the billionaires have been hawking other, dubious concerns, which Democratic foes of Prop. 40, including Newsom, have parroted without a lot of scrutiny. For instance, the claim that Prop. 40 will end up costing California money because billionaires will flee the state, and that this would be terrible for its economy.
Former US Rep. Katie Porter, who lost her recent bid for governor, posted a video (https://www.facebook.com/katieporterca/videos/ive-spent-my-career-arguing-that-we-should-demand-bold-change-that-improves-fami/2321734451928570/) of her top three reasons to vote against Prop. 40. To paraphrase: It doesn’t accomplish any of the big things Democrats have always longed for, such as Medicare for All; It’s “big bucks for Big Insurance;” and “It’s a one-time tax that would create long-term harms” by driving “hundreds of billions in potential tax revenues out of California.”
Her first reason is clearly ridiculous. The second is misleading: State legislators would sort out the details but, per the legislative analyst, 90 percent of the tax revenue would have to be spent on “health care services for the public.” To the extent this would “line the pockets of health-care executives,” as Porter put it, well, that’s a function of America’s dysfunctional health care system (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2024/12/toll-health-insurance-industry-profits-claim-denials-delays-care-brian-thompson-unitedhealth-luigi-mangione-physicians-national-health-program/), which Prop. 40 wasn’t designed to fix. But the alternative, proponents say, is to leave millions of low-income Californians, including many children, without health insurance, and put tens of thousands of health care providers out of work.
Her third talking point is echoed by other opponents, including Newsom, who has close ties to the Getty clan and is likely running for president, which means he needs billionaires in his corner. This one is straight from the No on 40 playbook: the notion that if the measure passes, these captains of industry will pull up stakes and depart for other jurisdictions, crippling the tax base and stifling California’s engine of innovation. Early on, a handful of billionaires announced their intention to leave. “The departure of these individuals alone,” the No on 40 campaign asserted, “is estimated to remove $536 billion, or nearly 30 percent of aggregate billionaire wealth, from the tax base.” This claim, though, is based on an analysis (https://www.hoover.org/press/californias-proposed-billionaire-tax-will-cost-state-estimated-25-billion-hoover-study-finds) by the conservative Hoover Institution that prompted a detailed rebuttal from the economists who helped write Prop. 40, arguing that the Hoover study is deeply flawed (https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c15504/c15504.pdf).
There are other, more basic problems with the notion that significant wealth flight will occur and that it will harm California and stifle innovation. As I’ve written elsewhere (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/california-billionaire-tax-billionaires-wealth-gap-unrealized-gains-rich-possible-fair/), the choice of whether to stay or go also depends on many factors unrelated to taxation, and nobody can accurately predict how most billionaires would react if Prop. 40 passed. The people making such predictions either have an agenda or are “delusional,” the former chief economist for California’s tax authority told me.
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, an outlier, has made clear he’ll stay put, and says he has no problem paying whatever taxes the state may impose. It’s a “privilege,” he told CBS News.
“I’m not afraid of paying taxes. I’m just afraid of being poor,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told @jolingkent (https://x.com/jolingkent?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw), as he explained why it would be a “privilege” to pay some $8 billion in taxes under California’s Proposition 40 – a one-time, 5% state tax on the net worth of California's… pic.twitter.com/SR3amOK1Om (https://t.co/SR3amOK1Om)
- CBS Sunday Morning 🌞 (@CBSSunday) October 19, 2026 (https://x.com/CBSSunday/status/2112234190284435529?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)
Of course, most of these tech billionaires weren’t wealthy when they started out—Huang once worked as a dishwasher (https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/magazines/panache/one-decision-that-made-jensen-huang-worth-185-billion-nvidia-nearly-went-bankrupt-in-1996-then-a-risky-bet-helped-build-its-ai-dominance/articleshow/135016538.cms?from=mdr) at Denny’s. New scrappy founders will come around and start ventures with or without the help of their predecessors. And even if all of California’s billionaires (Forbes counts 255 (https://www.forbes.com/lists/richest-in-each-state/)) were to leave and quit investing in new Silicon Valley companies, there’d still be tons of money available. The data firm Altrata, which tracks global wealth trends, estimates there are well over 22,000 ultra-high net worth individuals—people with net assets of $30 million and up—in San Francisco and Los Angeles alone. And investment, of course, can come from anywhere.
Rep. Ro Khanna doesn’t buy the claim that billionaires would flee over a 5 percent wealth tax: “They know that that is total propaganda.”
Finally, billionaire wealth is not a significant part of California’s tax base. In op-eds opposing Prop. 40, writers have pointed to the tax contributions of the state’s richest 1 percent—Newsom has even cited the top 10 percent . But billionaires comprise another realm entirely, and they already, by and large, have gone out of their way (https://www.propublica.org/article/the-secret-irs-files-trove-of-never-before-seen-records-reveal-how-the-wealthiest-avoid-income-tax) to ensure that only the tiniest sliver of their true economic income, and that of their companies, is subject to tax. Take Peter Thiel, one of the handful who say they’re already done with California. He famously used outrageous tactics (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) to accumulate more than $5 billion in a Roth IRA, a tax-free retirement account (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2022/02/retirement-savings-plans-favor-rich-wealth-gap-tax-incentives-portman-cardin-congress-secure-act/) designed for middle-class earners.
Newsom and others claim that, because billionaire wealth is portable, any wealth tax should be imposed at the federal level, not the state level, but as I made abundantly clear in my earlier piece, “How to Tax a Billionaire (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/california-billionaire-tax-billionaires-wealth-gap-unrealized-gains-rich-possible-fair/),” a federal wealth tax is never going to fly. Not, at least, without radical changes in the Supreme Court.
Besides, billionaires have done tremendously well in California, whose tech industry was built on a foundation (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2013/10/timeline-technology-silicon-valley-government-subsidies/) of publicly funded innovation. According to Forbes , Mark Zuckerberg’s net assets grew from $64.4 billion in 2023 to $214.6 billion on Thursday—an untaxed 233 percent gain in less than three years. If you’d put $1 in the S&P 500 in September 2023, and reinvested the dividends, it would have been worth about $1.80 in September 2026.
Would billionaires really turn tail over a paltry 5 percent tax?
At a recent event in San Francisco, I posed that question to Silicon Valley congressman Ro Khanna, whose support for Prop. 40 has made him persona non grata, he told me, among the tech billionaires in his district. “They know that that is total propaganda,” Khanna replied. “The AI revolution is happening in the Bay Area—it’s not happening in Miami or Austin. More wealth continues to pile into Silicon Valley than people know what to do with. One-third of the nation’s wealth is in my district and the 50-mile area around it. So the idea that investment is going to leave is just counter to every point of data that we have.”
Prop. 40 may be less than ideal, but it would at least break the glass and create a precedent for taxing runaway wealth.
“The reason they don’t want to pay the tax is they don’t want to pay the tax,” he continued. “They simply believe they’re entitled to this wealth…that they have, through their own labor, earned every penny, because they somehow are better than the rest of us.”
So, sure, there are legitimate quibbles, and maybe Prop. 40 isn’t the greatest thing, but it does at least break the glass. It creates a precedent for taxing wealth, which is what the billionaires fear most. In the end, their argument mainly boils down to greed. They don’t need this money. The reality, as I learned while researching my 2021 book, Jackpot (http://www.readjackpot.com/) , is that the nation’s richest men—and they are mostly men—are engaged in an epic yacht-measuring contest, literal and figurative.
And they don’t know how to stop.

California Billionaires May Well Prevail in Their Quest to Block a State Wealth Tax
They’re spending a fortune to spread fear about Prop. 40 and push countermeasures—with help from Gov. Gavin Newsom.
