Greed is on the California ballot, and it appears to be winning.
For a while, Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax initiative, which is supported by the state Democratic Party but opposed by many unions and prominent Democrats, was polling well. The notion of taxing the excessive wealth of the super-rich, or the basis of that wealth—the “paper profits” on a sea of unsold investments—has become increasingly popular across the nation. Nobody much likes taxation, but the way the economic spoils are distributed just isn’t working out well for most Americans, whose costs of living are growing faster than their wages, even as the wealth of the 0.00001 percent goes completely haywire (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/05/why-billionaires-pay-less-taxes-zucman-saez-jeff-bezos-irs-breaks-income-wealth/).
Add to that the specter of a wealthy, hyper-transactional president openly using his office (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/corruption-midterms-data-centers-epstein-stock-trading-pharma-texas-hinojosa-ossoff-sand/) to enrich himself, and his family and friends, often at taxpayer expense. The public, too, is finally starting to grasp the full extent to which our billionaires, most notably Elon Musk, are using their largely untaxed and godlike fortunes (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/04/us-federal-tax-system-progressive-oligarchy-rich-capital-unrealized-gains-wealth-inheritance-dynasty/) for political gain: dictating our ballot choices, messing with elections (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/elon-musk-is-the-midterms-biggest-disinformation-risk/), harming the nation (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/08/gao-report-doge-elon-musk-overstated-savings-wall-receipts-waste-fraud-cost/), and dodging accountability (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/05/oligarchy-tax-evasion-avoidance-irs-powerless-enforcement-books-blind-spot-excerpt-jeffrey-winters/).
If Prop. 40 passes, it would be the first-ever tax on excessive wealth, as opposed to income, in the United States. It would place a one-time, 5 percent levy on the net assets of California residents in excess of $1 billion. The measure, put forth by a health workers union to plug holes in the state Medicaid and education budgets created by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, immediately raised the hackles of California’s three-comma club, whose members tend to be allergic to taxation.
The claim that losing 250 billionaires would kill the state tax base and stifle innovation is laughable. They pay minimal taxes, and there are tens of thousands of Californians worth $30 million and up.
These moguls, led by Google co-founder Sergey Brin (who now claims residence in Nevada), started a group called Building a Better California (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/), which they’ve bankrolled to the tune of $333 million—about 0.1 percent of the combined net worth of its top 5 backers (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/technology/proposition-40-california-billionaire-tax.html): Brin, Google’s Steve Schmidt, venture capitalist John Doerr, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, and investor Vinod Khosla. The group has blanketed the state political landscape with anti-Prop 40 advertising and propaganda. It also bankrolled two poison pill initiatives, Props. 41 and 42, that we’ll talk about in a minute.
There are legitimate critiques of Prop. 40: Voter initiatives are a lousy way to do tax policy. Maybe it won’t bring in as much cash as projected. It’ll be challenged in court. (What isn’t?) Voters might conflate it with another measure, Prop. 3, that would extend an existing tax on income in excess of $371,000 ($742,000 for joint filers) to fund public education.
One big (valid) gripe about Prop. 40 is that it’s one-and-done. The California Teachers Union, for instance, says it opposes the measure on the grounds that it “will not provide the sustainable and long-lasting funding that our schools and communities deserve.” Such arguments are politically safe for Democratic politicians such as Xavier Becerra—who will almost certainly replace Gavin Newsom as governor, and who opposes Prop. 40 (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/2026/07/31/becerra-announces-positions-on-key-november-ballot-measures/) (though, in true weasel fashion, he has declined to take a position on the competing propositions, 41 and 42). The fact that most of the Prop. 40 revenues are earmarked for health care also may have miffed some of the other unions that oppose it (https://www.wsj.com/politics/california-billionaire-tax-democratic-party-f4729c1d?st=99MAWA&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink), and that would prefer some of the money go toward their own interests.
But the billionaires have been hawking other, dubious concerns, which Democratic foes of Prop. 40, including Newsom, have parroted without a lot of scrutiny. For instance, the claim that Prop. 40 will end up costing California money because billionaires will flee the state, and that this would be terrible for its economy.
Former US Rep. Katie Porter, who lost her recent bid for governor, posted a video (https://www.facebook.com/katieporterca/videos/ive-spent-my-career-arguing-that-we-should-demand-bold-change-that-improves-fami/2321734451928570/) of her top three reasons to vote against Prop. 40. To paraphrase: It doesn’t accomplish any of the big things Democrats have always longed for, such as Medicare for All; It’s “big bucks for Big Insurance;” and “It’s a one-time tax that would create long-term harms” by driving “hundreds of billions in potential tax revenues out of California.”
Her first reason is clearly ridiculous. The second is misleading: State legislators would sort out the details but, per the legislative analyst, 90 percent of the tax revenue would have to be spent on “health care services for the public.” To the extent this would “line the pockets of health-care executives,” as Porter put it, well, that’s a function of America’s dysfunctional health care system (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2024/12/toll-health-insurance-industry-profits-claim-denials-delays-care-brian-thompson-unitedhealth-luigi-mangione-physicians-national-health-program/), which Prop. 40 wasn’t designed to fix. But the alternative, proponents say, is to leave millions of low-income Californians, including many children, without health insurance, and put tens of thousands of health care providers out of work.
Her third talking point is echoed by other opponents, including Newsom, who has close ties to the Getty clan and is likely running for president, which means he needs billionaires in his corner. This one is straight from the No on 40 playbook: the notion that if the measure passes, these captains of industry will pull up stakes and depart for other jurisdictions, crippling the tax base and stifling California’s engine of innovation. Early on, a handful of billionaires announced their intention to leave. “The departure of these individuals alone,” the No on 40 campaign asserted, “is estimated to remove $536 billion, or nearly 30 percent of aggregate billionaire wealth, from the tax base.” This claim, though, is based on an analysis (https://www.hoover.org/press/californias-proposed-billionaire-tax-will-cost-state-estimated-25-billion-hoover-study-finds) by the conservative Hoover Institution that prompted a detailed rebuttal from the economists who helped write Prop. 40, arguing that the Hoover study is deeply flawed (https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c15504/c15504.pdf).
There are other, more basic problems with the notion that significant wealth flight will occur and that it will harm California and stifle innovation. As I’ve written elsewhere (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/california-billionaire-tax-billionaires-wealth-gap-unrealized-gains-rich-possible-fair/), the choice of whether to stay or go also depends on many factors unrelated to taxation, and nobody can accurately predict how most billionaires would react if Prop. 40 passed. The people making such predictions either have an agenda or are “delusional,” the former chief economist for California’s tax authority told me.
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, an outlier, has made clear he’ll stay put, and says he has no problem paying whatever taxes the state may impose. It’s a “privilege,” he told CBS News.
“I’m not afraid of paying taxes. I’m just afraid of being poor,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told @jolingkent (https://x.com/jolingkent?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw), as he explained why it would be a “privilege” to pay some $8 billion in taxes under California’s Proposition 40 – a one-time, 5% state tax on the net worth of California's… pic.twitter.com/SR3amOK1Om (https://t.co/SR3amOK1Om)
- CBS Sunday Morning 🌞 (@CBSSunday) October 19, 2026 (https://x.com/CBSSunday/status/2112234190284435529?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)
Of course, most of these tech billionaires weren’t wealthy when they started out—Huang once worked as a dishwasher (https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/magazines/panache/one-decision-that-made-jensen-huang-worth-185-billion-nvidia-nearly-went-bankrupt-in-1996-then-a-risky-bet-helped-build-its-ai-dominance/articleshow/135016538.cms?from=mdr) at Denny’s. New scrappy founders will come around and start ventures with or without the help of their predecessors. And even if all of California’s billionaires (Forbes counts 255 (https://www.forbes.com/lists/richest-in-each-state/)) were to leave and quit investing in new Silicon Valley companies, there’d still be tons of money available. The data firm Altrata, which tracks global wealth trends, estimates there are well over 22,000 ultra-high net worth individuals—people with net assets of $30 million and up—in San Francisco and Los Angeles alone. And investment, of course, can come from anywhere.
Rep. Ro Khanna doesn’t buy the claim that billionaires would flee over a 5 percent wealth tax: “They know that that is total propaganda.”
Finally, billionaire wealth is not a significant part of California’s tax base. In op-eds opposing Prop. 40, writers have pointed to the tax contributions of the state’s richest 1 percent—Newsom has even cited the top 10 percent . But billionaires comprise another realm entirely, and they already, by and large, have gone out of their way (https://www.propublica.org/article/the-secret-irs-files-trove-of-never-before-seen-records-reveal-how-the-wealthiest-avoid-income-tax) to ensure that only the tiniest sliver of their true economic income, and that of their companies, is subject to tax. Take Peter Thiel, one of the handful who say they’re already done with California. He famously used outrageous tactics (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) to accumulate more than $5 billion in a Roth IRA, a tax-free retirement account (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2022/02/retirement-savings-plans-favor-rich-wealth-gap-tax-incentives-portman-cardin-congress-secure-act/) designed for middle-class earners.
Newsom and others claim that, because billionaire wealth is portable, any wealth tax should be imposed at the federal level, not the state level, but as I made abundantly clear in my earlier piece, “How to Tax a Billionaire (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/california-billionaire-tax-billionaires-wealth-gap-unrealized-gains-rich-possible-fair/),” a federal wealth tax is never going to fly. Not, at least, without radical changes in the Supreme Court.
Besides, billionaires have done tremendously well in California, whose tech industry was built on a foundation (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2013/10/timeline-technology-silicon-valley-government-subsidies/) of publicly funded innovation. According to Forbes , Mark Zuckerberg’s net assets grew from $64.4 billion in 2023 to $214.6 billion on Thursday—an untaxed 233 percent gain in less than three years. If you’d put $1 in the S&P 500 in September 2023, and reinvested the dividends, it would have been worth about $1.80 in September 2026.
Would billionaires really turn tail over a paltry 5 percent tax?
At a recent event in San Francisco, I posed that question to Silicon Valley congressman Ro Khanna, whose support for Prop. 40 has made him persona non grata, he told me, among the tech billionaires in his district. “They know that that is total propaganda,” Khanna replied. “The AI revolution is happening in the Bay Area—it’s not happening in Miami or Austin. More wealth continues to pile into Silicon Valley than people know what to do with. One-third of the nation’s wealth is in my district and the 50-mile area around it. So the idea that investment is going to leave is just counter to every point of data that we have.”
Prop. 40 may be less than ideal, but it would at least break the glass and create a precedent for taxing runaway wealth.
“The reason they don’t want to pay the tax is they don’t want to pay the tax,” he continued. “They simply believe they’re entitled to this wealth…that they have, through their own labor, earned every penny, because they somehow are better than the rest of us.”
So, sure, there are legitimate quibbles, and maybe Prop. 40 isn’t the greatest thing, but it does at least break the glass. It creates a precedent for taxing wealth, which is what the billionaires fear most. In the end, their argument mainly boils down to greed. They don’t need this money. The reality, as I learned while researching my 2021 book, Jackpot (http://www.readjackpot.com/) , is that the nation’s richest men—and they are mostly men—are engaged in an epic yacht-measuring contest, literal and figurative.
And they don’t know how to stop.

Greed is on the California ballot, and it appears to be winning.
For a while, Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax initiative, which is supported by the state Democratic Party but opposed by many unions and prominent Democrats, was polling well. The notion of taxing the excessive wealth of the super-rich, or the basis of that wealth—the “paper profits” on a sea of unsold investments—has become increasingly popular across the nation. Nobody much likes taxation, but the way the economic spoils are distributed just isn’t working out well for most Americans, whose costs of living are growing faster than their wages, even as the wealth of the 0.00001 percent goes completely haywire (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/05/why-billionaires-pay-less-taxes-zucman-saez-jeff-bezos-irs-breaks-income-wealth/).
Add to that the specter of a wealthy, hyper-transactional president openly using his office (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/corruption-midterms-data-centers-epstein-stock-trading-pharma-texas-hinojosa-ossoff-sand/) to enrich himself, and his family and friends, often at taxpayer expense. The public, too, is finally starting to grasp the full extent to which our billionaires, most notably Elon Musk, are using their largely untaxed and godlike fortunes (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/04/us-federal-tax-system-progressive-oligarchy-rich-capital-unrealized-gains-wealth-inheritance-dynasty/) for political gain: dictating our ballot choices, messing with elections (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/elon-musk-is-the-midterms-biggest-disinformation-risk/), harming the nation (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/08/gao-report-doge-elon-musk-overstated-savings-wall-receipts-waste-fraud-cost/), and dodging accountability (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/05/oligarchy-tax-evasion-avoidance-irs-powerless-enforcement-books-blind-spot-excerpt-jeffrey-winters/).
If Prop. 40 passes, it would be the first-ever tax on excessive wealth, as opposed to income, in the United States. It would place a one-time, 5 percent levy on the net assets of California residents in excess of $1 billion. The measure, put forth by a health workers union to plug holes in the state Medicaid and education budgets created by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, immediately raised the hackles of California’s three-comma club, whose members tend to be allergic to taxation.
The claim that losing 250 billionaires would kill the state tax base and stifle innovation is laughable. They pay minimal taxes, and there are tens of thousands of Californians worth $30 million and up.
These moguls, led by Google co-founder Sergey Brin (who now claims residence in Nevada), started a group called Building a Better California (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/), which they’ve bankrolled to the tune of $333 million—about 0.1 percent of the combined net worth of its top 5 backers (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/technology/proposition-40-california-billionaire-tax.html): Brin, Google’s Steve Schmidt, venture capitalist John Doerr, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, and investor Vinod Khosla. The group has blanketed the state political landscape with anti-Prop 40 advertising and propaganda. It also bankrolled two poison pill initiatives, Props. 41 and 42, that we’ll talk about in a minute.
There are legitimate critiques of Prop. 40: Voter initiatives are a lousy way to do tax policy. Maybe it won’t bring in as much cash as projected. It’ll be challenged in court. (What isn’t?) Voters might conflate it with another measure, Prop. 3, that would extend an existing tax on income in excess of $371,000 ($742,000 for joint filers) to fund public education.
One big (valid) gripe about Prop. 40 is that it’s one-and-done. The California Teachers Union, for instance, says it opposes the measure on the grounds that it “will not provide the sustainable and long-lasting funding that our schools and communities deserve.” Such arguments are politically safe for Democratic politicians such as Xavier Becerra—who will almost certainly replace Gavin Newsom as governor, and who opposes Prop. 40 (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/2026/07/31/becerra-announces-positions-on-key-november-ballot-measures/) (though, in true weasel fashion, he has declined to take a position on the competing propositions, 41 and 42). The fact that most of the Prop. 40 revenues are earmarked for health care also may have miffed some of the other unions that oppose it (https://www.wsj.com/politics/california-billionaire-tax-democratic-party-f4729c1d?st=99MAWA&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink), and that would prefer some of the money go toward their own interests.
But the billionaires have been hawking other, dubious concerns, which Democratic foes of Prop. 40, including Newsom, have parroted without a lot of scrutiny. For instance, the claim that Prop. 40 will end up costing California money because billionaires will flee the state, and that this would be terrible for its economy.
Former US Rep. Katie Porter, who lost her recent bid for governor, posted a video (https://www.facebook.com/katieporterca/videos/ive-spent-my-career-arguing-that-we-should-demand-bold-change-that-improves-fami/2321734451928570/) of her top three reasons to vote against Prop. 40. To paraphrase: It doesn’t accomplish any of the big things Democrats have always longed for, such as Medicare for All; It’s “big bucks for Big Insurance;” and “It’s a one-time tax that would create long-term harms” by driving “hundreds of billions in potential tax revenues out of California.”
Her first reason is clearly ridiculous. The second is misleading: State legislators would sort out the details but, per the legislative analyst, 90 percent of the tax revenue would have to be spent on “health care services for the public.” To the extent this would “line the pockets of health-care executives,” as Porter put it, well, that’s a function of America’s dysfunctional health care system (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2024/12/toll-health-insurance-industry-profits-claim-denials-delays-care-brian-thompson-unitedhealth-luigi-mangione-physicians-national-health-program/), which Prop. 40 wasn’t designed to fix. But the alternative, proponents say, is to leave millions of low-income Californians, including many children, without health insurance, and put tens of thousands of health care providers out of work.
Her third talking point is echoed by other opponents, including Newsom, who has close ties to the Getty clan and is likely running for president, which means he needs billionaires in his corner. This one is straight from the No on 40 playbook: the notion that if the measure passes, these captains of industry will pull up stakes and depart for other jurisdictions, crippling the tax base and stifling California’s engine of innovation. Early on, a handful of billionaires announced their intention to leave. “The departure of these individuals alone,” the No on 40 campaign asserted, “is estimated to remove $536 billion, or nearly 30 percent of aggregate billionaire wealth, from the tax base.” This claim, though, is based on an analysis (https://www.hoover.org/press/californias-proposed-billionaire-tax-will-cost-state-estimated-25-billion-hoover-study-finds) by the conservative Hoover Institution that prompted a detailed rebuttal from the economists who helped write Prop. 40, arguing that the Hoover study is deeply flawed (https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c15504/c15504.pdf).
There are other, more basic problems with the notion that significant wealth flight will occur and that it will harm California and stifle innovation. As I’ve written elsewhere (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/california-billionaire-tax-billionaires-wealth-gap-unrealized-gains-rich-possible-fair/), the choice of whether to stay or go also depends on many factors unrelated to taxation, and nobody can accurately predict how most billionaires would react if Prop. 40 passed. The people making such predictions either have an agenda or are “delusional,” the former chief economist for California’s tax authority told me.
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, an outlier, has made clear he’ll stay put, and says he has no problem paying whatever taxes the state may impose. It’s a “privilege,” he told CBS News.
“I’m not afraid of paying taxes. I’m just afraid of being poor,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told @jolingkent (https://x.com/jolingkent?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw), as he explained why it would be a “privilege” to pay some $8 billion in taxes under California’s Proposition 40 – a one-time, 5% state tax on the net worth of California's… pic.twitter.com/SR3amOK1Om (https://t.co/SR3amOK1Om)
- CBS Sunday Morning 🌞 (@CBSSunday) October 19, 2026 (https://x.com/CBSSunday/status/2112234190284435529?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)
Of course, most of these tech billionaires weren’t wealthy when they started out—Huang once worked as a dishwasher (https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/magazines/panache/one-decision-that-made-jensen-huang-worth-185-billion-nvidia-nearly-went-bankrupt-in-1996-then-a-risky-bet-helped-build-its-ai-dominance/articleshow/135016538.cms?from=mdr) at Denny’s. New scrappy founders will come around and start ventures with or without the help of their predecessors. And even if all of California’s billionaires (Forbes counts 255 (https://www.forbes.com/lists/richest-in-each-state/)) were to leave and quit investing in new Silicon Valley companies, there’d still be tons of money available. The data firm Altrata, which tracks global wealth trends, estimates there are well over 22,000 ultra-high net worth individuals—people with net assets of $30 million and up—in San Francisco and Los Angeles alone. And investment, of course, can come from anywhere.
Rep. Ro Khanna doesn’t buy the claim that billionaires would flee over a 5 percent wealth tax: “They know that that is total propaganda.”
Finally, billionaire wealth is not a significant part of California’s tax base. In op-eds opposing Prop. 40, writers have pointed to the tax contributions of the state’s richest 1 percent—Newsom has even cited the top 10 percent . But billionaires comprise another realm entirely, and they already, by and large, have gone out of their way (https://www.propublica.org/article/the-secret-irs-files-trove-of-never-before-seen-records-reveal-how-the-wealthiest-avoid-income-tax) to ensure that only the tiniest sliver of their true economic income, and that of their companies, is subject to tax. Take Peter Thiel, one of the handful who say they’re already done with California. He famously used outrageous tactics (https://www.propublica.org/article/lord-of-the-roths-how-tech-mogul-peter-thiel-turned-a-retirement-account-for-the-middle-class-into-a-5-billion-dollar-tax-free-piggy-bank) to accumulate more than $5 billion in a Roth IRA, a tax-free retirement account (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2022/02/retirement-savings-plans-favor-rich-wealth-gap-tax-incentives-portman-cardin-congress-secure-act/) designed for middle-class earners.
Newsom and others claim that, because billionaire wealth is portable, any wealth tax should be imposed at the federal level, not the state level, but as I made abundantly clear in my earlier piece, “How to Tax a Billionaire (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/california-billionaire-tax-billionaires-wealth-gap-unrealized-gains-rich-possible-fair/),” a federal wealth tax is never going to fly. Not, at least, without radical changes in the Supreme Court.
Besides, billionaires have done tremendously well in California, whose tech industry was built on a foundation (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2013/10/timeline-technology-silicon-valley-government-subsidies/) of publicly funded innovation. According to Forbes , Mark Zuckerberg’s net assets grew from $64.4 billion in 2023 to $214.6 billion on Thursday—an untaxed 233 percent gain in less than three years. If you’d put $1 in the S&P 500 in September 2023, and reinvested the dividends, it would have been worth about $1.80 in September 2026.
Would billionaires really turn tail over a paltry 5 percent tax?
At a recent event in San Francisco, I posed that question to Silicon Valley congressman Ro Khanna, whose support for Prop. 40 has made him persona non grata, he told me, among the tech billionaires in his district. “They know that that is total propaganda,” Khanna replied. “The AI revolution is happening in the Bay Area—it’s not happening in Miami or Austin. More wealth continues to pile into Silicon Valley than people know what to do with. One-third of the nation’s wealth is in my district and the 50-mile area around it. So the idea that investment is going to leave is just counter to every point of data that we have.”
Prop. 40 may be less than ideal, but it would at least break the glass and create a precedent for taxing runaway wealth.
“The reason they don’t want to pay the tax is they don’t want to pay the tax,” he continued. “They simply believe they’re entitled to this wealth…that they have, through their own labor, earned every penny, because they somehow are better than the rest of us.”
So, sure, there are legitimate quibbles, and maybe Prop. 40 isn’t the greatest thing, but it does at least break the glass. It creates a precedent for taxing wealth, which is what the billionaires fear most. In the end, their argument mainly boils down to greed. They don’t need this money. The reality, as I learned while researching my 2021 book, Jackpot (http://www.readjackpot.com/) , is that the nation’s richest men—and they are mostly men—are engaged in an epic yacht-measuring contest, literal and figurative.
And they don’t know how to stop.

Greed is on the California ballot, and it appears to be winning.
For a while, Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax initiative, which is supported by the state Democratic Party but opposed by many unions and prominent Democrats, was polling well. The notion of taxing the excessive wealth of the super-rich, or the basis of that wealth—the “paper profits” on a sea of unsold investments—has become increasingly popular across the nation. Nobody much likes taxation, but the way the economic spoils are distributed just isn’t working out well for most Americans, whose costs of living are growing faster than their wages, even as the wealth of the 0.00001 percent goes completely haywire (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/05/why-billionaires-pay-less-taxes-zucman-saez-jeff-bezos-irs-breaks-income-wealth/).
Add to that the specter of a wealthy, hyper-transactional president openly using his office (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/corruption-midterms-data-centers-epstein-stock-trading-pharma-texas-hinojosa-ossoff-sand/) to enrich himself, and his family and friends, often at taxpayer expense. The public, too, is finally starting to grasp the full extent to which our billionaires, most notably Elon Musk, are using their largely untaxed and godlike fortunes (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/04/us-federal-tax-system-progressive-oligarchy-rich-capital-unrealized-gains-wealth-inheritance-dynasty/) for political gain: dictating our ballot choices, messing with elections (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/10/elon-musk-is-the-midterms-biggest-disinformation-risk/), harming the nation (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/08/gao-report-doge-elon-musk-overstated-savings-wall-receipts-waste-fraud-cost/), and dodging accountability (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/05/oligarchy-tax-evasion-avoidance-irs-powerless-enforcement-books-blind-spot-excerpt-jeffrey-winters/).
If Prop. 40 passes, it would be the first-ever tax on excessive wealth, as opposed to income, in the United States. It would place a one-time, 5 percent levy on the net assets of California residents in excess of $1 billion. The measure, put forth by a health workers union to plug holes in the state Medicaid and education budgets created by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill, immediately raised the hackles of California’s three-comma club, whose members tend to be allergic to taxation.
The claim that losing 250 billionaires would kill the state tax base and stifle innovation is laughable. They pay minimal taxes, and there are tens of thousands of Californians worth $30 million and up.
These moguls, led by Google co-founder Sergey Brin (who now claims residence in Nevada), started a group called Building a Better California (https://www.buildingabetterca.org/), which they’ve bankrolled to the tune of $333 million—about 0.1 percent of the combined net worth of its top 5 backers (https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/technology/proposition-40-california-billionaire-tax.html): Brin, Google’s Steve Schmidt, venture capitalist John Doerr, Stripe co-founder Patrick Collison, and investor Vinod Khosla. The group has blanketed the state political landscape with anti-Prop 40 advertising and propaganda. It also bankrolled two poison pill initiatives, Props. 41 and 42, that we’ll talk about in a minute.
There are legitimate critiques of Prop. 40: Voter initiatives are a lousy way to do tax policy. Maybe it won’t bring in as much cash as projected. It’ll be challenged in court. (What isn’t?) Voters might conflate it with another measure, Prop. 3, that would extend an existing tax on income in excess of $371,000 ($742,000 for joint filers) to fund public education.
One big (valid) gripe about Prop. 40 is that it’s one-and-done. The California Teachers Union, for instance, says it opposes the measure on the grounds that it “will not provide the sustainable and long-lasting funding that our schools and communities deserve.” Such arguments are politically safe for Democratic politicians such as Xavier Becerra—who will almost certainly replace Gavin Newsom as governor, and who opposes Prop. 40 (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/2026/07/31/becerra-announces-positions-on-key-november-ballot-measures/) (though, in true weasel fashion, he has declined to take a position on the competing propositions, 41 and 42). The fact that most of the Prop. 40 revenues are earmarked for health care also may have miffed some of the other unions that oppose it (https://www.wsj.com/politics/california-billionaire-tax-democratic-party-f4729c1d?st=99MAWA&reflink=desktopwebshare_permalink), and that would prefer some of the money go toward their own interests.
But the billionaires have been hawking other, dubious concerns, which Democratic foes of Prop. 40, including Newsom, have parroted without a lot of scrutiny. For instance, the claim that Prop. 40 will end up costing California money because billionaires will flee the state, and that this would be terrible for its economy.
Former US Rep. Katie Porter, who lost her recent bid for governor, posted a video (https://www.facebook.com/katieporterca/videos/ive-spent-my-career-arguing-that-we-should-demand-bold-change-that-improves-fami/2321734451928570/) of her top three reasons to vote against Prop. 40. To paraphrase: It doesn’t accomplish any of the big things Democrats have always longed for, such as Medicare for All; It’s “big bucks for Big Insurance;” and “It’s a one-time tax that would create long-term harms” by driving “hundreds of billions in potential tax revenues out of California.”
Her first reason is clearly ridiculous. The second is misleading: State legislators would sort out the details but, per the legislative analyst, 90 percent of the tax revenue would have to be spent on “health care services for the public.” To the extent this would “line the pockets of health-care executives,” as Porter put it, well, that’s a function of America’s dysfunctional health care system (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2024/12/toll-health-insurance-industry-profits-claim-denials-delays-care-brian-thompson-unitedhealth-luigi-mangione-physicians-national-health-program/), which Prop. 40 wasn’t designed to fix. But the alternative, proponents say, is to leave millions of low-income Californians, including many children, without health insurance, and put tens of thousands of health care providers out of work.
Her third talking point is echoed by other opponents, including Newsom, who has close ties to the Getty clan and is likely running for president, which means he needs billionaires in his corner. This one is straight from the No on 40 playbook: the notion that if the measure passes, these captains of industry will pull up stakes and depart for other jurisdictions, crippling the tax base and stifling California’s engine of innovation. Early on, a handful of billionaires announced their intention to leave. “The departure of these individuals alone,” the No on 40 campaign asserted, “is estimated to remove $536 billion, or nearly 30 percent of aggregate billionaire wealth, from the tax base.” This claim, though, is based on an analysis (https://www.hoover.org/press/californias-proposed-billionaire-tax-will-cost-state-estimated-25-billion-hoover-study-finds) by the conservative Hoover Institution that prompted a detailed rebuttal from the economists who helped write Prop. 40, arguing that the Hoover study is deeply flawed (https://www.nber.org/system/files/chapters/c15504/c15504.pdf).
There are other, more basic problems with the notion that significant wealth flight will occur and that it will harm California and stifle innovation. As I’ve written elsewhere (https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/06/california-billionaire-tax-billionaires-wealth-gap-unrealized-gains-rich-possible-fair/), the choice of whether to stay or go also depends on many factors unrelated to taxation, and nobody can accurately predict how most billionaires would react if Prop. 40 passed. The people making such predictions either have an agenda or are “delusional,” the former chief economist for California’s tax authority told me.
Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, an outlier, has made clear he’ll stay put, and says he has no problem paying whatever taxes the state may impose. It’s a “privilege,” he told CBS News.
“I’m not afraid of paying taxes. I’m just afraid of being poor,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told @jolingkent (https://x.com/jolingkent?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw), as he explained why it would be a “privilege” to pay some $8 billion in taxes under California’s Proposition 40 – a one-time, 5% state tax on the net worth of California's… pic.twitter.com/SR3amOK1Om (https://t.co/SR3amOK1Om)

Of course, most of these tech billionaires weren’t wealthy when they started out—Huang once worked as a dishwasher (https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/magazines/panache/one-decision-that-made-jensen-huang-worth-185-billion-nvidia-nearly-went-bankrupt-in-1996-then-a-risky-bet-helped-build-its-ai-dominance/articleshow/135016538.cms?from=mdr) at Denny’s. New scrappy founders will come around and start ventures with or without the help of their predecessors. And even if all of California’s billionaires (Forbes counts 255 (https://www.forbes.com/lists/richest-in-each-state/)) were to leave and quit investing in new Silicon Valley companies, there’d still be tons of money available. The data firm Altrata, which tracks global wealth trends, estimates there are well over 22,000 ultra-high net worth individuals—people with net assets of $30 million and up—in San Francisco and Los Angeles alone. And investment, of course, can come from anywhere.
Rep. Ro Khanna doesn’t buy the claim that billionaires would flee over a 5 percent wealth tax: “They know that that is total propaganda.”
Finally, billionaire wealth is not a significant part of California’s tax base. In op-eds opposing Prop. 40, writers have pointed to the tax contributions of the state’s richest 1 percent—Newsom has even cited the top 10 percent . Prop. 40 may be less than ideal, but it would at least break the glass and create a precedent for taxing runaway wealth.
“The reason they don’t want to pay the tax is they don’t want to pay the tax,” he continued. “They simply believe they’re entitled to this wealth…that they have, through their own labor, earned every penny, because they somehow are better than the rest of us.”

saner, more inclusive tax policies. It’s worth watching if you’ve got the time.
The billionaires’ quest to hoard wealth and fight taxes tooth and nail is, in Payne’s view, an addiction. “What happens when people start doing drugs?” she told the crowd. “The drug becomes disproportionately important. They need more of the drug to get the same high. Their emotional baseline changes and their braking system is less effective. So, the next time a billionaire says they don’t want to be taxed, you just say to yourself, that’s the addiction talking.”
This addiction to hoarding is what prompted the inclusion of the competing propositions I mentioned. Both are poison pills. Prop. 41 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), in addition to imposing audits on future tax initiatives, would nullify any state tax whose revenues are excluded (as Prop. 40 would be) from the spending limit voters passed in 1979. Because the two propositions are in conflict, the legislative analyst notes, Prop. 40 would likely be voided if both measures pass and Prop. 41 gets more yes votes.
The same goes for Prop. 42 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), which Newsom also supports. This measure subverts Prop. 40 by prohibiting retroactive taxes. (Prop. 40 would apply to anyone who was a California resident on January 1, 2026.) Prop. 42 also prohibits any future state tax on “personal property, business interests, and financial assets”—namely, wealth—“including assets in retirement and investment accounts.”
The billionaires are quite sneaky here. By calling out retirement savings, they are implying that ordinary people’s nest eggs are at risk. That’s really not true, but Newsom, shamefully, hasembraced the fearmongering (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/): “We all agree that Californians deserve to have their retirement and life savings protected from new state taxes,” he said in a statement released by Prop. 42’s backers.
One never knows what will happen on Election Day, and polls are often unreliable, but the latest reputable ones, with days to go, are suggesting that Prop. 40 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-wealth-tax-polls-2026.html) and Prop. 41 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-prop-41-tax-audits-polls-2026.html?searchResultPosition=1) are likely to go down, whereas Prop. 42 (https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/polls/california-prop-42-personal-property-tax-polls-2026.html?searchResultPosition=1) may well squeak by.
So much for California dreamin’.

The billionaires’ quest to hoard wealth and fight taxes tooth and nail is, in Payne’s view, an addiction. “What happens when people start doing drugs?” she told the crowd. “The drug becomes disproportionately important. This addiction to hoarding is what prompted the inclusion of the competing propositions I mentioned. Both are poison pills. Prop. 41 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=41&year=2026), in addition to imposing audits on future tax initiatives, would nullify any state tax whose revenues are excluded (as Prop. 40 would be) from the spending limit voters passed in 1979. Because the two propositions are in conflict, the legislative analyst notes, Prop. 40 would likely be voided if both measures pass and Prop. 41 gets more yes votes.
The same goes for Prop. 42 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=42&year=2026), which Newsom also supports. This measure subverts Prop. 40 by prohibiting retroactive taxes. (Prop. 40 would apply to anyone who was a California resident on January 1, 2026.) Prop. 42 also prohibits any future state tax on “personal property, business interests, and financial assets”—namely, wealth—“including assets in retirement and investment accounts.”
The billionaires are quite sneaky here. By calling out retirement savings, they are implying that ordinary people’s nest eggs are at risk. Seven in ten voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem. Majorities back extending taxes on high incomes and borrowing for housing, the billionaire tax is a toss-up, and Becerra leads by 24 points even though fewer than half of voters say California is on the right track.
SAN DIEGO: California’s election is being decided at the kitchen table. Seven in ten likely voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem - cost of living (38%), housing (19%), and the economy and jobs (12%) - and their ballot choices suggest they want the bill sent to the top, according to a new poll by AIMSA, distributed by Quadratín California.
The survey of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 19–24, finds a consistent pattern on the ballot. Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property. The pattern suggests voters favor measures whose cost falls on a narrow group of taxpayers or that expand access to housing, and resist taxes that could reach their own households.
“The message from California voters is clear: affordability and economic opportunity come first,” said Tayde Aburto, President of the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce (HISCEC). “Behind these numbers are families working to make ends meet and small business owners navigating rising costs.”
The most closely watched measure, Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires, leads 50% to 44%, a margin the report places within the poll’s range of error. Its outcome is likely to resonate well beyond California.
Politically, the poll reveals a paradox: only 45% of voters say the state is headed in the right direction, yet Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 58% to 34%. President Donald Trump’s approval among the state’s likely voters is just 29%, compared with 50% for Governor Gavin Newsom, suggesting the race is being shaped as much by views of Washington as of Sacramento. The race appears largely settled: 24% have already voted and only 13% say they could change their minds.
For voters of Mexican origin, the affordability squeeze crosses the border. Seventy-one percent of Latino voters were born in the U.S., yet 29% send remittances to their country of origin and 34% chose to answer in Spanish: for nearly three in ten, one household budget supports two economies. Mexican-origin voters back Becerra 66% to 25%, while Latinos of other origins vote almost exactly like the state as a whole (58% to 32%). Tax the Top, Fix Housing, Back Becerra: Cost of Living Drives California’s Vote, AIMSA Poll Finds

Seven in ten voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem. Majorities back extending taxes on high incomes and borrowing for housing, the billionaire tax is a toss-up, and Becerra leads by 24 points even though fewer than half of voters say California is on the right track.
SAN DIEGO: California’s election is being decided at the kitchen table. Seven in ten likely voters name an economic issue as the state’s top problem - cost of living (38%), housing (19%), and the economy and jobs (12%) - and their ballot choices suggest they want the bill sent to the top, according to a new poll by AIMSA, distributed by Quadratín California.
The survey of 2,000 likely voters, conducted October 19–24, finds a consistent pattern on the ballot. Proposition 3, which extends taxes on high incomes, has 56% support; Proposition 37, loans for middle-income homebuyers, 59%; and Proposition 1, affordable housing bonds, 54%. At the same time, 50% back Proposition 42, which would ban state taxes on personal property. The pattern suggests voters favor measures whose cost falls on a narrow group of taxpayers or that expand access to housing, and resist taxes that could reach their own households.
“The message from California voters is clear: affordability and economic opportunity come first,” said Tayde Aburto, President of the Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce (HISCEC). “Behind these numbers are families working to make ends meet and small business owners navigating rising costs.”
The most closely watched measure, Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires, leads 50% to 44%, a margin the report places within the poll’s range of error. Its outcome is likely to resonate well beyond California.
Politically, the poll reveals a paradox: only 45% of voters say the state is headed in the right direction, yet Democrat Xavier Becerra leads Republican Steve Hilton 58% to 34%. President Donald Trump’s approval among the state’s likely voters is just 29%, compared with 50% for Governor Gavin Newsom, suggesting the race is being shaped as much by views of Washington as of Sacramento. The race appears largely settled: 24% have already voted and only 13% say they could change their minds.
For voters of Mexican origin, the affordability squeeze crosses the border. Seventy-one percent of Latino voters were born in the U.S., yet 29% send remittances to their country of origin and 34% chose to answer in Spanish: for nearly three in ten, one household budget supports two economies. Mexican-origin voters back Becerra 66% to 25%, while Latinos of other origins vote almost exactly like the state as a whole (58% to 32%). And while 52% of Latino voters approve of Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, only 41% approve of the U.S.–Mexico relationship.
Leo Espinoza, President of Quadratín California, said the findings place the voices of Latino and Mexican-origin voters - a community with strong ties to Mexico - at the center of the conversation about the state’s future.
A second wave of the AIMSA survey, in the field since October 26, will show whether the billionaire tax and other close measures move in the final stretch. The full report, with results by region, age, sex and party, all 14 propositions, and the module on Latino and Mexican-origin voters, is available to journalists. Jesús Javier García Ruiz, Director of AIMSA, is available for interviews.
Methodology
AIMSA independently directed, conducted and financed the study; Quadratín California is the media partner and HISCEC supports outreach. The survey combines 1,200 SMS-to-web interviews linked to the voter file and 800 online panel interviews, in English and Spanish, across seven regions, with an oversample of 800 Latino voters. The 95% credibility interval is ±3 points statewide and ±4.5 among Latinos, larger for subgroups such as voters of Mexican origin. Results are not a forecast.

California voters: Deeply blue, deeply restless
Sixteen statewide polling projects show a clear frontrunner for governor—and a far less settled electorate on taxes, housing and the state’s direction.
Jon Cohen (https://substack.com/@jcpolls)
Nov 02, 2026
Share
The October polls give Xavier Becerra a consistent lead. They give the next governor a much more complicated assignment.
Every one of the 14 governor ballot readings in this October collection puts Democrat Xavier Becerra ahead of Republican Steve Hilton. Yet in PPIC’s latest survey, 73% of likely voters say their income is not keeping up with prices. 67% call housing affordability a big problem. A majority say California is headed in the wrong direction. PPIC’s full likely-voter tables (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf) put those findings alongside a 61% vote for Becerra.
A state can be reliably Democratic and deeply dissatisfied at the same time.
That is the strongest through-line in a sweep of 16 statewide polling projects in our October collection. Their reported samples total 18,962 respondent records. These are samples across different surveys, not 18,962 distinct people or one giant California poll. The newly obtained Hoover crosstabs supply the sample size missing from the Boskin–Rivers article. Three field periods began in September; the Patriotic Millionaires release does not disclose its interview dates. The count and its limits are spelled out below.
The bigger story is an electorate whose party preference is clearer than its policy preferences—and whose patience with the cost of living appears thin.
The agreement on the governor’s race is broad. The agreement on its margin is weaker.
The narrowest result is a Hilton campaign internal by David Wolfson (https://nypost.com/2026/10/04/us-news/xavier-becerras-lead-over-steve-hilton-shrinks-to-5-6-points-in-new-california-governor-poll) , fielded October 1–2, showing Becerra ahead by 6 points. Its limited public methodology warrants caution. The other published leads range from 10 points to 28. That spread matters: a common leader is stronger evidence than a common estimate of the eventual winning margin.
Different pollsters interviewing different electorates at different times cannot establish that Becerra’s lead has grown. They do establish that his advantage appears across a wide variety of polls, including surveys from PPIC, Emerson, SurveyUSA, Manhattan Institute and Republican pollster McLaughlin.
The party coalitions help explain the consistency. PPIC has Becerra winning 92% of Democrats and Hilton 89% of Republicans. Its independents favor Becerra 54% to 41%. Manhattan Institute (https://manhattan.institute/article/californias-contradictions-survey-analysis-of-2026-voter-preferences-statewide-and-in-los-angeles) likewise finds overwhelming party loyalty and an independent edge for Becerra, 48% to 39%.
Hoover / YouGov adds a 56%–36% Becerra lead among 983 likely voters. Its full-sample governor result is 52%–35% among 1,124 respondents after excluding people who definitely will not vote. Those are different populations within one survey, not two independent polls. Hoover governor tables, PDF p.7 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
ActiVote’s October 31 release reinforces that picture: Becerra leads 63%–37% among 400 likely voters, the same whole-number split as its earlier wave. Independents favor him 71%–29%; Hilton leads rural voters 56%–44%. Becerra takes 81% among voters under 30, versus 54% among those 65 and older. This opt-in app poll publishes a two-candidate result and no exact subgroup Ns, so the splits are descriptive. ActiVote release and full crosstabs. (https://www.activote.net/polls/2026/ca-governor/)
Even here, the labels require care. The Citrin Center/POLITICO survey, conducted by TrueDot, assigns party leaners to the parties. Its much smaller remaining group of pure independents and others—just 75 likely voters—is divided about 30%–30%, with 36% undecided. That is a different group from a broad independent category. Treating the two as interchangeable would manufacture a disagreement.
The new Berkeley IGS governor crosstabs (https://escholarship.org/content/qt9sg025d9/qt9sg025d9.pdf#page=8) provide an unusually direct test of the distinction between a vote and an endorsement. Becerra leads 61%–34% statewide. Even among voters who view him somewhat unfavorably, 47% choose him, compared with 36% for Hilton. His support extends beyond his admirers; the question does not establish what drives their choice.
The same survey adds nuance to the prospect of California electing its first Latino governor. Among 400 Latino likely voters, 45% feel proud about that possibility. Yet only 25% agree it would reduce racial inequality, while 61% disagree. On whether it would help ease fears in the Latino community, they divide 40% agree to 43% disagree. Pride in a milestone can coexist with limited expectations about what it will deliver. IGS Latino crosstabs (https://escholarship.org/content/qt9sg025d9/qt9sg025d9.pdf#page=29)
The discontent is real—and it is bigger than a candidate matchup.
The affordability finding travels across surveys. SurveyUSA (https://results.surveyusa.com/client/PollReport.aspx?g=b118a915-559d-4669-b870-8a3eae933903) finds 43% of its 799 likely voters selecting the cost of living as the biggest issue facing California. AIMSA (https://wkow.marketminute.com/article/bizwire-2026-10-27-tax-the-top-fix-housing-back-becerra-cost-of-living-drives-californias-vote-aimsa-poll-finds) similarly puts living costs and housing at the top of its problem list.
The questions and poll designs differ. They point toward a common concern without producing a common number to average.
IGS shows how shared concern about prices can sit inside very different political agendas. Asked to select up to two top election issues, Becerra and Hilton supporters name the cost of living at almost identical rates: 33% and 34%. Their other priorities diverge sharply.
Fighting Trump administration policies is a top issue for 62% of Becerra supporters and 2% of Hilton supporters. Hilton supporters are far more likely to select taxes, immigration enforcement and public safety. An electorate can share a concern without agreeing on what government should do about it.
There is also a direct demand for a different governing direction. In the Citrin Center/POLITICO study (https://live-citrin-center.pantheon.berkeley.edu/the-citrin-center-x-politico-october-2026/) , 62% of registered voters want the next governor to take California in a different direction from Gavin Newsom’s policies. The same study’s likely-voter ballot favors Becerra 55% to 35%.
Those two findings do not tell us that every Becerra voter wants a break with Newsom. They do tell us how easily a winning Democratic coalition could be mistaken for an endorsement of the status quo.
For the next governor, the implication is substantial. The election may offer a strong partisan starting position. The public’s assessment of affordability and government performance would remain a separate test.
The policy ballot gives us a clearer view of that selectivity.
PPIC finds majorities favoring a housing bond, homebuyer loans and an extension of taxes on high incomes. It also finds majorities opposing the billionaire wealth tax, voter ID and the clinic-spending measure. Six of its 14 measures receive more than 50% Yes.
The new Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408) reinforces an important distinction: the high-income tax extension leads 54%–37%, while the billionaire tax trails 42%–50%. AIMSA also reports majority support for the income-tax extension and both housing measures.
That is a more useful picture than a statewide label such as “pro-tax” or “anti-tax.” Voters are being asked about different taxes, different uses of money and different rules. The results suggest campaigns should take those distinctions seriously. They do not isolate which feature of a proposal causes support or opposition.
Even within the same party category, support varies. PPIC finds 80% of Democrats backing the income-tax extension, compared with 64% backing the wealth tax. Among independents, the figures are 56% and 40%. A Democratic advantage in a candidate race leaves plenty of room for a policy fight.
The wealth tax is where the disagreements become impossible to ignore.
Among the eight likely-voter polls compared here, reported Yes ranges from 35% in Manhattan Institute to 50% in AIMSA. PPIC and IGS put it behind; SurveyUSA has a nearly even 44%–43% split. Hoover reports 47% Yes and 36% No. Seven of those eight likely-voter estimates put Yes below 50%.
Then come the three newer sources, each adding something different.
The LSE authors’ YouGov study (https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/usappblog/2026/10/28/income-tax-voter-partisan-divisions/) reports 58% support among California registered voters. Its fieldwork was earlier than PPIC’s and IGS’s. Its electorate is broader. The publication does not supply everything needed to align its question and party subgroups precisely with those other polls. It adds a distinctly more favorable reading of the proposal. It does not establish a late surge.
The Patriotic Millionaires release (https://patrioticmillionaires.org/perspectives/yougov-poll-of-california-millionaires/) reports 57% support among California millionaires. It adds evidence of support within a millionaire population. Millionaires are a much broader group than the billionaires targeted by the measure, and a millionaire sample cannot substitute for an electorate. Its support scale also differs from a conventional Yes/No ballot question.
The newly obtained Hoover / YouGov crosstabs accompanying the Boskin–Rivers article (https://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/p/what-californians-really-want) supply direct ballot tests. Among likely voters, Proposition 40 receives 47% Yes, 36% No and 16% unsure, with 982 responding. Proposition 41 stands at 38%–35%, with 981 responding; Proposition 42 is 40%–38%, with 980 responding. Blank or not-voted responses are retained. The wealth-tax question uses a short description of a one-time tax on billionaires, rather than the full ballot description. Hoover ballot tables, PDF pp.13, 15 and 17 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
The article’s joint table (https://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/p/what-californians-really-want) also places 29% in a group backing Proposition 40 without backing 41 or 42, and 18% in a group backing 40 and at least one of the others. Those combinations do not by themselves establish confusion. The crosstabs supply question wording and responding bases; exact field dates, recruitment, weighting and uncertainty estimates remain unreported.
Hoover also shows why a fairness grievance may coexist with doubts about execution. In its broader sample, 62% agree billionaires are not paying their fair share, while 67% believe billionaires will avoid this tax. In the published Democratic Party ID group, the figures are 83% and 72%, with 523 respondents on each question. These separate questions describe attitudes within the party; they do not identify what caused anyone’s tax vote. Hoover attitude tables, PDF pp.28 and 36 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
Self-described understanding needs care as well. Across the broader sample, 81% say they understand Proposition 40 very or somewhat well. A separate question finds 52% select assets as the tax base, while 22% select income and 26% are unsure. Responding bases are 1,154 and 1,151, respectively. The aggregate gap does not identify which individual voters misunderstand it. Hoover understanding tables, PDF pp.10 and 19 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
One striking unresolved difference sits inside the party columns: the LSE article reports roughly 45% Republican support for the wealth tax. PPIC reports 18%; IGS reports 6% among registered Republicans. Different party definitions, voter screens and question presentation could matter. The available evidence does not tell us how much each explains. Averaging the three would bury the question we should be asking.
Amid the topline disagreement, one pattern recurs: younger voters are more receptive to the wealth tax.
PPIC has 70% Yes among people ages 18–34 and 33% among those 55 and older. IGS and Manhattan Institute show the same age ordering, using different age bands. PPIC also finds a substantial tenure gap: 65% among renters, 39% among owners.
These are associations, not a demonstration that renting or being young causes someone’s vote. Age, income and homeownership overlap. The recurring pattern nevertheless gives campaigns a concrete coalition to examine—and makes the composition of the eventual electorate especially consequential.
Hoover repeats the age ordering: 65% of respondents under 30 say Yes to Proposition 40, compared with 37% among those 65 and older. The respective unweighted bases are 124 and 351. These demographic columns exclude people who definitely will not vote; they are not likely-voter-only age groups. Hoover age tables, PDF p.13 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
The age divide also runs through confidence in implementation. Asked whether California could accurately value private companies, art and collectibles, 72% under 30 are confident, versus 36% among those 65 and older. Those unweighted bases are 131 and 354. The question covers the broader sample. These parallel age patterns suggest a role for expectations about government capacity, without establishing that confidence causes the tax vote. Hoover asset-valuation tables, PDF p.23 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
IGS adds a related housing-priority divide. Promoting housing development makes its top-two election-issue list for 13% of voters under 30, compared with 3% among ages 50–64 and 3% among those 65 and older. The unweighted bases are 162, 503 and 734 respectively. This asks about a particular priority on a crowded list; it is a different measure from PPIC’s question about whether housing affordability is a big problem. IGS age crosstabs (https://escholarship.org/content/qt9sg025d9/qt9sg025d9.pdf#page=16)
Voter ID supplies a second lesson in reading the disagreements rather than smoothing them away. PPIC and IGS put Proposition 39 clearly behind. SurveyUSA puts it ahead 49%–42%. IVP’s published ballot-description result is 43%–40%, with 17% undecided. M3’s published table shows just Yes and No, 47% and 53% respectively.
IVP’s own survey (https://ivn.us/new-ca-poll-voter-id-measure-leads-today-its-undecided-voters-point-the-other-way/) also illustrates the distance between a general idea and a particular initiative: 62% support voter ID with a free card, while 43% say Yes after the ballot description. That comparison involves different content and question order. It is not a randomized estimate of a wording effect. It is a reason to read the question before treating a headline as a forecast.
The House polls expose different local versions of a Democratic advantage.
USC’s four newly released district polls put Democrats ahead on each initial House ballot, by 8 to 14 points. Those four districts are not a representative sample of California. Their crosstabs nevertheless show why a broad statewide label can conceal important differences.
In CA-22, Villegas leads overall while trailing Valadao 33%–62% among No Party Preference voters after the follow-up question to undecideds. In CA-06, Pan leads that category 55%–44%, even though Kiley is running with a No Party Preference label. Registration, ideology and candidate preference cannot be treated as interchangeable.
The economic crosstabs sharpen the broader piece’s central tension. In CA-22, 50% call gas prices a major financial problem. That group favors Villegas 68%–29%. In CA-48, voters reporting a major gas-price problem favor von Wilpert 63%–22%. Financial distress and Democratic support coexist within these groups. The questions do not identify whom voters blame for prices or show that financial pressure caused their candidate choice. USC crosstabs (https://www.thedemocracylab.com/pdfs/capolling.pdf#page=93)
USC also finds a difference within the recalled Trump coalition in CA-22. Among Latino likely voters who say they voted for Trump in 2024, 16% back Villegas and 78% Valadao. Among White likely voters recalling a Trump vote, those figures are 7% and 93%. These are conditional subgroups with unpublished Ns, based on recalled past votes and current intentions. They suggest a difference in Republican consolidation, rather than measuring validated defections since 2024. USC crosstabs (https://www.thedemocracylab.com/pdfs/capolling.pdf#page=94)
Candidate support also leaves policy questions open. In CA-22, Villegas leads the initial ballot 52%–41%, while opposition to a hypothetical California data-center moratorium exceeds support, 45%–34%, summing the published strong and somewhat responses. That is a district-level comparison of separate questions. It does not identify individual voters holding both positions, and the moratorium is not a ballot initiative. Neither new release adds fresh vote estimates for the statewide measures. USC policy results (https://www.thedemocracylab.com/pdfs/capolling.pdf#page=32)
What comes next
Becerra’s repeated lead makes a Democratic win the consistent implication of the published ballot tests. The variation in margins and methods still matters, and the polls do not determine the result.
The ballot measures offer a less settled landscape. Housing and the income-tax extension draw support in multiple surveys. The wealth tax and voter ID face much more divergent readings. For the wealth tax, the recurring age divide adds a turnout question to a persuasion question.
There is also a legal wrinkle beyond the polling. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) , Proposition 40 could be prevented from taking effect if 41 or 42 also passes with more Yes votes and a court finds a conflict. That is conditional, not an automatic cancellation rule. Understanding the combination of votes matters alongside understanding each measure separately.
Finally, the statewide partisan advantage offers little reassurance to every incumbent. In Los Angeles, IGS’s city-only poll (https://ca-times.brightspotcdn.com/ed/23/a4f13a5c44e0b7e61a6a0faae036/tabulations-from-late-october-poll-of-la-city-likely-voters.pdf) has Karen Bass and Nithya Raman tied at 40%. That is a different electorate and race, kept separate from the statewide count. It is a useful reminder that a blue state contains plenty of competitive arguments over who should govern it.
The next governor may inherit a Democratic advantage. These polls suggest he would not inherit a satisfied electorate.

California voters: Deeply blue, deeply restless
Sixteen statewide polling projects show a clear frontrunner for governor—and a far less settled electorate on taxes, housing and the state’s direction.
Jon Cohen (https://substack.com/@jcpolls)
Nov 02, 2026
Share
The October polls give Xavier Becerra a consistent lead. They give the next governor a much more complicated assignment.
Every one of the 14 governor ballot readings in this October collection puts Democrat Xavier Becerra ahead of Republican Steve Hilton. Yet in PPIC’s latest survey, 73% of likely voters say their income is not keeping up with prices. 67% call housing affordability a big problem. A majority say California is headed in the wrong direction. PPIC’s full likely-voter tables (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf) put those findings alongside a 61% vote for Becerra.
A state can be reliably Democratic and deeply dissatisfied at the same time.
That is the strongest through-line in a sweep of 16 statewide polling projects in our October collection. Their reported samples total 18,962 respondent records. These are samples across different surveys, not 18,962 distinct people or one giant California poll. The newly obtained Hoover crosstabs supply the sample size missing from the Boskin–Rivers article. Three field periods began in September; the Patriotic Millionaires release does not disclose its interview dates. The count and its limits are spelled out below.
The bigger story is an electorate whose party preference is clearer than its policy preferences—and whose patience with the cost of living appears thin.
The agreement on the governor’s race is broad. The agreement on its margin is weaker.
The narrowest result is a Hilton campaign internal by David Wolfson (https://nypost.com/2026/10/04/us-news/xavier-becerras-lead-over-steve-hilton-shrinks-to-5-6-points-in-new-california-governor-poll) , fielded October 1–2, showing Becerra ahead by 6 points. Its limited public methodology warrants caution. The other published leads range from 10 points to 28. That spread matters: a common leader is stronger evidence than a common estimate of the eventual winning margin.
Different pollsters interviewing different electorates at different times cannot establish that Becerra’s lead has grown. They do establish that his advantage appears across a wide variety of polls, including surveys from PPIC, Emerson, SurveyUSA, Manhattan Institute and Republican pollster McLaughlin.
The party coalitions help explain the consistency. PPIC has Becerra winning 92% of Democrats and Hilton 89% of Republicans. Its independents favor Becerra 54% to 41%. Manhattan Institute (https://manhattan.institute/article/californias-contradictions-survey-analysis-of-2026-voter-preferences-statewide-and-in-los-angeles) likewise finds overwhelming party loyalty and an independent edge for Becerra, 48% to 39%.
Hoover / YouGov adds a 56%–36% Becerra lead among 983 likely voters. Its full-sample governor result is 52%–35% among 1,124 respondents after excluding people who definitely will not vote. Those are different populations within one survey, not two independent polls. Hoover governor tables, PDF p.7 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
ActiVote’s October 31 release reinforces that picture: Becerra leads 63%–37% among 400 likely voters, the same whole-number split as its earlier wave. Independents favor him 71%–29%; Hilton leads rural voters 56%–44%. Becerra takes 81% among voters under 30, versus 54% among those 65 and older. This opt-in app poll publishes a two-candidate result and no exact subgroup Ns, so the splits are descriptive. ActiVote release and full crosstabs. (https://www.activote.net/polls/2026/ca-governor/)
Even here, the labels require care. The Citrin Center/POLITICO survey, conducted by TrueDot, assigns party leaners to the parties. Its much smaller remaining group of pure independents and others—just 75 likely voters—is divided about 30%–30%, with 36% undecided. That is a different group from a broad independent category. Treating the two as interchangeable would manufacture a disagreement.
The new Berkeley IGS governor crosstabs (https://escholarship.org/content/qt9sg025d9/qt9sg025d9.pdf#page=8) provide an unusually direct test of the distinction between a vote and an endorsement. Becerra leads 61%–34% statewide. Even among voters who view him somewhat unfavorably, 47% choose him, compared with 36% for Hilton. His support extends beyond his admirers; the question does not establish what drives their choice.
The same survey adds nuance to the prospect of California electing its first Latino governor. Among 400 Latino likely voters, 45% feel proud about that possibility. Yet only 25% agree it would reduce racial inequality, while 61% disagree. On whether it would help ease fears in the Latino community, they divide 40% agree to 43% disagree. Pride in a milestone can coexist with limited expectations about what it will deliver. IGS Latino crosstabs (https://escholarship.org/content/qt9sg025d9/qt9sg025d9.pdf#page=29)
The discontent is real—and it is bigger than a candidate matchup.
The affordability finding travels across surveys. SurveyUSA (https://results.surveyusa.com/client/PollReport.aspx?g=b118a915-559d-4669-b870-8a3eae933903) finds 43% of its 799 likely voters selecting the cost of living as the biggest issue facing California. AIMSA (https://wkow.marketminute.com/article/bizwire-2026-10-27-tax-the-top-fix-housing-back-becerra-cost-of-living-drives-californias-vote-aimsa-poll-finds) similarly puts living costs and housing at the top of its problem list.
The questions and poll designs differ. They point toward a common concern without producing a common number to average.
IGS shows how shared concern about prices can sit inside very different political agendas. Asked to select up to two top election issues, Becerra and Hilton supporters name the cost of living at almost identical rates: 33% and 34%. Their other priorities diverge sharply.
Fighting Trump administration policies is a top issue for 62% of Becerra supporters and 2% of Hilton supporters. Hilton supporters are far more likely to select taxes, immigration enforcement and public safety. An electorate can share a concern without agreeing on what government should do about it.
There is also a direct demand for a different governing direction. In the Citrin Center/POLITICO study (https://live-citrin-center.pantheon.berkeley.edu/the-citrin-center-x-politico-october-2026/) , 62% of registered voters want the next governor to take California in a different direction from Gavin Newsom’s policies. The same study’s likely-voter ballot favors Becerra 55% to 35%.
Those two findings do not tell us that every Becerra voter wants a break with Newsom. They do tell us how easily a winning Democratic coalition could be mistaken for an endorsement of the status quo.
For the next governor, the implication is substantial. The election may offer a strong partisan starting position. The public’s assessment of affordability and government performance would remain a separate test.
The policy ballot gives us a clearer view of that selectivity.
PPIC finds majorities favoring a housing bond, homebuyer loans and an extension of taxes on high incomes. It also finds majorities opposing the billionaire wealth tax, voter ID and the clinic-spending measure. Six of its 14 measures receive more than 50% Yes.
The new Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408) reinforces an important distinction: the high-income tax extension leads 54%–37%, while the billionaire tax trails 42%–50%. AIMSA also reports majority support for the income-tax extension and both housing measures.
That is a more useful picture than a statewide label such as “pro-tax” or “anti-tax.” Voters are being asked about different taxes, different uses of money and different rules. The results suggest campaigns should take those distinctions seriously. They do not isolate which feature of a proposal causes support or opposition.
Even within the same party category, support varies. PPIC finds 80% of Democrats backing the income-tax extension, compared with 64% backing the wealth tax. Among independents, the figures are 56% and 40%. A Democratic advantage in a candidate race leaves plenty of room for a policy fight.
The wealth tax is where the disagreements become impossible to ignore.
Among the eight likely-voter polls compared here, reported Yes ranges from 35% in Manhattan Institute to 50% in AIMSA. PPIC and IGS put it behind; SurveyUSA has a nearly even 44%–43% split. Hoover reports 47% Yes and 36% No. Seven of those eight likely-voter estimates put Yes below 50%.
Then come the three newer sources, each adding something different.

### California Decides
#### What Californians Really Want
In addition to serving as a Senior Fellow, Douglas Rivers is the chief scientist at the global polling firm YouGov PLC.
He teamed up with Senior Fellow Michael J. Boskin to analyze the results of two recent YouGov polls examining how Californians, and Americans nationally, feel about taxes and spending.
As it turns out, despite California’s high taxes and government spending, the poll found that Golden State residents actually have views on taxation similar to those of residents in other states, at least when it comes to their own tax burden: They would prefer lower federal and state income tax rates.
Turning to California’s Proposition 40, proposing a wealth tax on billionaires, Rivers and Boskin find a conflicted voting public and suggest that “the majority of Californians believe the state has a spending problem, not a tax problem.”
The survey also found considerable pessimism from Californians about the state’s ability to administer a wealth tax, even if they favor the idea in theory.
While the findings are interesting in that they suggest California policy realities diverge considerably from voters’ preferences, the authors conclude that political change in Sacramento is not likely—at least not yet.
