California voters: Deeply blue, deeply restless
Sixteen statewide polling projects show a clear frontrunner for governor—and a far less settled electorate on taxes, housing and the state’s direction.
Jon Cohen (https://substack.com/@jcpolls)
Nov 02, 2026
Share
The October polls give Xavier Becerra a consistent lead. They give the next governor a much more complicated assignment.
Every one of the 14 governor ballot readings in this October collection puts Democrat Xavier Becerra ahead of Republican Steve Hilton. Yet in PPIC’s latest survey, 73% of likely voters say their income is not keeping up with prices. 67% call housing affordability a big problem. A majority say California is headed in the wrong direction. PPIC’s full likely-voter tables (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf) put those findings alongside a 61% vote for Becerra.
A state can be reliably Democratic and deeply dissatisfied at the same time.
That is the strongest through-line in a sweep of 16 statewide polling projects in our October collection. Their reported samples total 18,962 respondent records. These are samples across different surveys, not 18,962 distinct people or one giant California poll. The newly obtained Hoover crosstabs supply the sample size missing from the Boskin–Rivers article. Three field periods began in September; the Patriotic Millionaires release does not disclose its interview dates. The count and its limits are spelled out below.
The bigger story is an electorate whose party preference is clearer than its policy preferences—and whose patience with the cost of living appears thin.
The agreement on the governor’s race is broad. The agreement on its margin is weaker.
The narrowest result is a Hilton campaign internal by David Wolfson (https://nypost.com/2026/10/04/us-news/xavier-becerras-lead-over-steve-hilton-shrinks-to-5-6-points-in-new-california-governor-poll) , fielded October 1–2, showing Becerra ahead by 6 points. Its limited public methodology warrants caution. The other published leads range from 10 points to 28. That spread matters: a common leader is stronger evidence than a common estimate of the eventual winning margin.
Different pollsters interviewing different electorates at different times cannot establish that Becerra’s lead has grown. They do establish that his advantage appears across a wide variety of polls, including surveys from PPIC, Emerson, SurveyUSA, Manhattan Institute and Republican pollster McLaughlin.
The party coalitions help explain the consistency. PPIC has Becerra winning 92% of Democrats and Hilton 89% of Republicans. Its independents favor Becerra 54% to 41%. Manhattan Institute (https://manhattan.institute/article/californias-contradictions-survey-analysis-of-2026-voter-preferences-statewide-and-in-los-angeles) likewise finds overwhelming party loyalty and an independent edge for Becerra, 48% to 39%.
Hoover / YouGov adds a 56%–36% Becerra lead among 983 likely voters. Its full-sample governor result is 52%–35% among 1,124 respondents after excluding people who definitely will not vote. Those are different populations within one survey, not two independent polls. Hoover governor tables, PDF p.7 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
ActiVote’s October 31 release reinforces that picture: Becerra leads 63%–37% among 400 likely voters, the same whole-number split as its earlier wave. Independents favor him 71%–29%; Hilton leads rural voters 56%–44%. Becerra takes 81% among voters under 30, versus 54% among those 65 and older. This opt-in app poll publishes a two-candidate result and no exact subgroup Ns, so the splits are descriptive. ActiVote release and full crosstabs. (https://www.activote.net/polls/2026/ca-governor/)
Even here, the labels require care. The Citrin Center/POLITICO survey, conducted by TrueDot, assigns party leaners to the parties. Its much smaller remaining group of pure independents and others—just 75 likely voters—is divided about 30%–30%, with 36% undecided. That is a different group from a broad independent category. Treating the two as interchangeable would manufacture a disagreement.
The new Berkeley IGS governor crosstabs (https://escholarship.org/content/qt9sg025d9/qt9sg025d9.pdf#page=8) provide an unusually direct test of the distinction between a vote and an endorsement. Becerra leads 61%–34% statewide. Even among voters who view him somewhat unfavorably, 47% choose him, compared with 36% for Hilton. His support extends beyond his admirers; the question does not establish what drives their choice.
The same survey adds nuance to the prospect of California electing its first Latino governor. Among 400 Latino likely voters, 45% feel proud about that possibility. Yet only 25% agree it would reduce racial inequality, while 61% disagree. On whether it would help ease fears in the Latino community, they divide 40% agree to 43% disagree. Pride in a milestone can coexist with limited expectations about what it will deliver. IGS Latino crosstabs (https://escholarship.org/content/qt9sg025d9/qt9sg025d9.pdf#page=29)
The discontent is real—and it is bigger than a candidate matchup.
The affordability finding travels across surveys. SurveyUSA (https://results.surveyusa.com/client/PollReport.aspx?g=b118a915-559d-4669-b870-8a3eae933903) finds 43% of its 799 likely voters selecting the cost of living as the biggest issue facing California. AIMSA (https://wkow.marketminute.com/article/bizwire-2026-10-27-tax-the-top-fix-housing-back-becerra-cost-of-living-drives-californias-vote-aimsa-poll-finds) similarly puts living costs and housing at the top of its problem list.
The questions and poll designs differ. They point toward a common concern without producing a common number to average.
IGS shows how shared concern about prices can sit inside very different political agendas. Asked to select up to two top election issues, Becerra and Hilton supporters name the cost of living at almost identical rates: 33% and 34%. Their other priorities diverge sharply.
Fighting Trump administration policies is a top issue for 62% of Becerra supporters and 2% of Hilton supporters. Hilton supporters are far more likely to select taxes, immigration enforcement and public safety. An electorate can share a concern without agreeing on what government should do about it.
There is also a direct demand for a different governing direction. In the Citrin Center/POLITICO study (https://live-citrin-center.pantheon.berkeley.edu/the-citrin-center-x-politico-october-2026/) , 62% of registered voters want the next governor to take California in a different direction from Gavin Newsom’s policies. The same study’s likely-voter ballot favors Becerra 55% to 35%.
Those two findings do not tell us that every Becerra voter wants a break with Newsom. They do tell us how easily a winning Democratic coalition could be mistaken for an endorsement of the status quo.
For the next governor, the implication is substantial. The election may offer a strong partisan starting position. The public’s assessment of affordability and government performance would remain a separate test.
The policy ballot gives us a clearer view of that selectivity.
PPIC finds majorities favoring a housing bond, homebuyer loans and an extension of taxes on high incomes. It also finds majorities opposing the billionaire wealth tax, voter ID and the clinic-spending measure. Six of its 14 measures receive more than 50% Yes.
The new Berkeley IGS poll (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408) reinforces an important distinction: the high-income tax extension leads 54%–37%, while the billionaire tax trails 42%–50%. AIMSA also reports majority support for the income-tax extension and both housing measures.
That is a more useful picture than a statewide label such as “pro-tax” or “anti-tax.” Voters are being asked about different taxes, different uses of money and different rules. The results suggest campaigns should take those distinctions seriously. They do not isolate which feature of a proposal causes support or opposition.
Even within the same party category, support varies. PPIC finds 80% of Democrats backing the income-tax extension, compared with 64% backing the wealth tax. Among independents, the figures are 56% and 40%. A Democratic advantage in a candidate race leaves plenty of room for a policy fight.
The wealth tax is where the disagreements become impossible to ignore.
Among the eight likely-voter polls compared here, reported Yes ranges from 35% in Manhattan Institute to 50% in AIMSA. PPIC and IGS put it behind; SurveyUSA has a nearly even 44%–43% split. Hoover reports 47% Yes and 36% No. Seven of those eight likely-voter estimates put Yes below 50%.
Then come the three newer sources, each adding something different.
The LSE authors’ YouGov study (https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/usappblog/2026/10/28/income-tax-voter-partisan-divisions/) reports 58% support among California registered voters. Its fieldwork was earlier than PPIC’s and IGS’s. Its electorate is broader. The publication does not supply everything needed to align its question and party subgroups precisely with those other polls. It adds a distinctly more favorable reading of the proposal. It does not establish a late surge.
The Patriotic Millionaires release (https://patrioticmillionaires.org/perspectives/yougov-poll-of-california-millionaires/) reports 57% support among California millionaires. It adds evidence of support within a millionaire population. Millionaires are a much broader group than the billionaires targeted by the measure, and a millionaire sample cannot substitute for an electorate. Its support scale also differs from a conventional Yes/No ballot question.
The newly obtained Hoover / YouGov crosstabs accompanying the Boskin–Rivers article (https://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/p/what-californians-really-want) supply direct ballot tests. Among likely voters, Proposition 40 receives 47% Yes, 36% No and 16% unsure, with 982 responding. Proposition 41 stands at 38%–35%, with 981 responding; Proposition 42 is 40%–38%, with 980 responding. Blank or not-voted responses are retained. The wealth-tax question uses a short description of a one-time tax on billionaires, rather than the full ballot description. Hoover ballot tables, PDF pp.13, 15 and 17 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
The article’s joint table (https://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/p/what-californians-really-want) also places 29% in a group backing Proposition 40 without backing 41 or 42, and 18% in a group backing 40 and at least one of the others. Those combinations do not by themselves establish confusion. The crosstabs supply question wording and responding bases; exact field dates, recruitment, weighting and uncertainty estimates remain unreported.
Hoover also shows why a fairness grievance may coexist with doubts about execution. In its broader sample, 62% agree billionaires are not paying their fair share, while 67% believe billionaires will avoid this tax. In the published Democratic Party ID group, the figures are 83% and 72%, with 523 respondents on each question. These separate questions describe attitudes within the party; they do not identify what caused anyone’s tax vote. Hoover attitude tables, PDF pp.28 and 36 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
Self-described understanding needs care as well. Across the broader sample, 81% say they understand Proposition 40 very or somewhat well. A separate question finds 52% select assets as the tax base, while 22% select income and 26% are unsure. Responding bases are 1,154 and 1,151, respectively. The aggregate gap does not identify which individual voters misunderstand it. Hoover understanding tables, PDF pp.10 and 19 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
One striking unresolved difference sits inside the party columns: the LSE article reports roughly 45% Republican support for the wealth tax. PPIC reports 18%; IGS reports 6% among registered Republicans. Different party definitions, voter screens and question presentation could matter. The available evidence does not tell us how much each explains. Averaging the three would bury the question we should be asking.
Amid the topline disagreement, one pattern recurs: younger voters are more receptive to the wealth tax.
PPIC has 70% Yes among people ages 18–34 and 33% among those 55 and older. IGS and Manhattan Institute show the same age ordering, using different age bands. PPIC also finds a substantial tenure gap: 65% among renters, 39% among owners.
These are associations, not a demonstration that renting or being young causes someone’s vote. Age, income and homeownership overlap. The recurring pattern nevertheless gives campaigns a concrete coalition to examine—and makes the composition of the eventual electorate especially consequential.
Hoover repeats the age ordering: 65% of respondents under 30 say Yes to Proposition 40, compared with 37% among those 65 and older. The respective unweighted bases are 124 and 351. These demographic columns exclude people who definitely will not vote; they are not likely-voter-only age groups. Hoover age tables, PDF p.13 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
The age divide also runs through confidence in implementation. Asked whether California could accurately value private companies, art and collectibles, 72% under 30 are confident, versus 36% among those 65 and older. Those unweighted bases are 131 and 354. The question covers the broader sample. These parallel age patterns suggest a role for expectations about government capacity, without establishing that confidence causes the tax vote. Hoover asset-valuation tables, PDF p.23 (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1wcIDqdwpibyBfU0XiFXCM288uzUaMWRv/view?usp=drivesdk) .
IGS adds a related housing-priority divide. Promoting housing development makes its top-two election-issue list for 13% of voters under 30, compared with 3% among ages 50–64 and 3% among those 65 and older. The unweighted bases are 162, 503 and 734 respectively. This asks about a particular priority on a crowded list; it is a different measure from PPIC’s question about whether housing affordability is a big problem. IGS age crosstabs (https://escholarship.org/content/qt9sg025d9/qt9sg025d9.pdf#page=16)
Voter ID supplies a second lesson in reading the disagreements rather than smoothing them away. PPIC and IGS put Proposition 39 clearly behind. SurveyUSA puts it ahead 49%–42%. IVP’s published ballot-description result is 43%–40%, with 17% undecided. M3’s published table shows just Yes and No, 47% and 53% respectively.
IVP’s own survey (https://ivn.us/new-ca-poll-voter-id-measure-leads-today-its-undecided-voters-point-the-other-way/) also illustrates the distance between a general idea and a particular initiative: 62% support voter ID with a free card, while 43% say Yes after the ballot description. That comparison involves different content and question order. It is not a randomized estimate of a wording effect. It is a reason to read the question before treating a headline as a forecast.
The House polls expose different local versions of a Democratic advantage.
USC’s four newly released district polls put Democrats ahead on each initial House ballot, by 8 to 14 points. Those four districts are not a representative sample of California. Their crosstabs nevertheless show why a broad statewide label can conceal important differences.
In CA-22, Villegas leads overall while trailing Valadao 33%–62% among No Party Preference voters after the follow-up question to undecideds. In CA-06, Pan leads that category 55%–44%, even though Kiley is running with a No Party Preference label. Registration, ideology and candidate preference cannot be treated as interchangeable.
The economic crosstabs sharpen the broader piece’s central tension. In CA-22, 50% call gas prices a major financial problem. That group favors Villegas 68%–29%. In CA-48, voters reporting a major gas-price problem favor von Wilpert 63%–22%. Financial distress and Democratic support coexist within these groups. The questions do not identify whom voters blame for prices or show that financial pressure caused their candidate choice. USC crosstabs (https://www.thedemocracylab.com/pdfs/capolling.pdf#page=93)
USC also finds a difference within the recalled Trump coalition in CA-22. Among Latino likely voters who say they voted for Trump in 2024, 16% back Villegas and 78% Valadao. Among White likely voters recalling a Trump vote, those figures are 7% and 93%. These are conditional subgroups with unpublished Ns, based on recalled past votes and current intentions. They suggest a difference in Republican consolidation, rather than measuring validated defections since 2024. USC crosstabs (https://www.thedemocracylab.com/pdfs/capolling.pdf#page=94)
Candidate support also leaves policy questions open. In CA-22, Villegas leads the initial ballot 52%–41%, while opposition to a hypothetical California data-center moratorium exceeds support, 45%–34%, summing the published strong and somewhat responses. That is a district-level comparison of separate questions. It does not identify individual voters holding both positions, and the moratorium is not a ballot initiative. Neither new release adds fresh vote estimates for the statewide measures. USC policy results (https://www.thedemocracylab.com/pdfs/capolling.pdf#page=32)
What comes next
Becerra’s repeated lead makes a Democratic win the consistent implication of the published ballot tests. The variation in margins and methods still matters, and the polls do not determine the result.
The ballot measures offer a less settled landscape. Housing and the income-tax extension draw support in multiple surveys. The wealth tax and voter ID face much more divergent readings. For the wealth tax, the recurring age divide adds a turnout question to a persuasion question.
There is also a legal wrinkle beyond the polling. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) , Proposition 40 could be prevented from taking effect if 41 or 42 also passes with more Yes votes and a court finds a conflict. That is conditional, not an automatic cancellation rule. Understanding the combination of votes matters alongside understanding each measure separately.
Finally, the statewide partisan advantage offers little reassurance to every incumbent. In Los Angeles, IGS’s city-only poll (https://ca-times.brightspotcdn.com/ed/23/a4f13a5c44e0b7e61a6a0faae036/tabulations-from-late-october-poll-of-la-city-likely-voters.pdf) has Karen Bass and Nithya Raman tied at 40%. That is a different electorate and race, kept separate from the statewide count. It is a useful reminder that a blue state contains plenty of competitive arguments over who should govern it.
The next governor may inherit a Democratic advantage. These polls suggest he would not inherit a satisfied electorate.
What is in the count
This review covers 16 statewide polling projects in the October collection as of November 1, rather than claiming an exhaustive census of every California poll. Respondents may recur across surveys, and the samples include adults, registered voters, likely voters and millionaires. There is no meaningful combined margin of error.

### California Decides
#### What Californians Really Want
In addition to serving as a Senior Fellow, Douglas Rivers is the chief scientist at the global polling firm YouGov PLC.
He teamed up with Senior Fellow Michael J. Boskin to analyze the results of two recent YouGov polls examining how Californians, and Americans nationally, feel about taxes and spending.
As it turns out, despite California’s high taxes and government spending, the poll found that Golden State residents actually have views on taxation similar to those of residents in other states, at least when it comes to their own tax burden: They would prefer lower federal and state income tax rates.
Turning to California’s Proposition 40, proposing a wealth tax on billionaires, Rivers and Boskin find a conflicted voting public and suggest that “the majority of Californians believe the state has a spending problem, not a tax problem.”
The survey also found considerable pessimism from Californians about the state’s ability to administer a wealth tax, even if they favor the idea in theory.
While the findings are interesting in that they suggest California policy realities diverge considerably from voters’ preferences, the authors conclude that political change in Sacramento is not likely—at least not yet.

What Californians Really Want
As Election Day nears, voters aren’t clamoring for higher taxes or spending. A new poll shows surprising overlap with others across America.
By Michael J. Boskin (https://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/a/michael-j-boskin) and Douglas Rivers (https://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/a/douglas-rivers)
Thursday, October 29, 2026
23 3 Share
With the debates surrounding the proposed taxes on California’s November 3 ballot and the characterization of California as a high-tax, high-spending, heavy-welfare state, it may seem surprising that this is not what Californians really want.
JOIN THE COMMUNITY (http://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/subscribe)
In fact, Californians’ views on taxes and spending are quite similar to the views of the rest of the country in many dimensions. A careful look at their attitudes towards taxes and spending is necessary, so this month YouGov conducted parallel national and California surveys for us focused precisely on these issues.
Californians aren’t that different
Before turning to taxes, here is some of the evidence that California and the rest of the country are quite similar in how they feel about the future.
Optimism: Californians are 45 percent very or somewhat optimistic, versus 34 percent who are somewhat or very pessimistic. The corresponding figures nationally are 44 percent versus 35 percent. Contrary to conventional media narratives, young adults are the most optimistic, both nationally (48 to 32 percent) and in California (53 to 28 percent). The state’s Democrats are equally divided, as are independents, while Republicans, who comprise just a quarter of California’s registered voters, are overwhelmingly optimistic (67–16 percent). Perhaps this is because they support many of the policies pursued nationally by the Trump administration, which more than offsets their dissatisfaction with state policy.
What kind of economy? When asked about their preferred economic system, 15 percent of Californians say they prefer socialism and 2 percent communism, versus 16 percent and 2 percent nationally. There is a modest difference in that 42 percent of Californians prefer a mixed capitalist/socialist model versus 35 percent nationally, whereas nationally 35 percent prefer a pure capitalist model versus only 25 percent in California.
A “vote” poster combines with a Grateful Dead symbol at a Democratic Party rally Oct. 23 in San Francisco. [Heather Diehl—Associated Press] Interestingly, while no sex, race, or age group favors socialism by more than 17 percent, black Californians favor capitalism least and overwhelmingly favor a mixed capitalist-socialist model, whereas Asians are the least favorable to socialism at 9 percent. While the majority of Democrats in the state favor a mixed system (54 percent), they favor socialism to capitalism by 3 to 1, whereas Republicans overwhelmingly favor capitalism (64 percent to 4 percent for socialism), with independents favoring capitalism by 2 to 1 over socialism (28–13 percent), but a plurality favors a mixed system (43 percent). We prefaced these questions with a series that gave various definitions and features of capitalism and socialism, so the possibility that different groups have different ideas about the nature of each of these systems is somewhat mitigated. At the national level, the results are similar. Notable differences include middle-aged and older respondents being even more favorable to capitalism over a mixed model than in California.
A spending problem : Of those agreeing or disagreeing, Californians are even more in agreement that their state has a spending problem, not a revenue problem, by 48 percent to 20 percent, whereas nationally the figures are 43 percent vs. 19 percent. In both cases, the pattern holds across all ages, but is even more pronounced for older respondents, still more so in California.
Anti-business: One area where California differs is that slightly more Californians think their state is more anti-business than pro-business, with sharp differences by age: the two youngest groups think the state is more pro-business and the two older groups, more anti-business. Politically, Democrats believe the state is more pro-business by 37–14 percent, Republicans lean the other way, more strongly, at 15–56 percent, with independents leaning anti- by 12 points. Nationally, the picture is dramatically different: 41 percent believe their state is pro-business vs. only 15 percent anti-business.
Californians want lower taxes for themselves
It turns out Californians really don’t like high taxes, including high tax rates, especially (unsurprisingly) when they believe they may wind up paying them now or in the future.
Californians believe the federal personal income tax should be reduced: 47 percent want it decreased vs. 16 percent who want it increased (26 percent want it kept the same and 12 percent are unsure). Nationally, the views are even more lopsided: 14 percent would like it increased, 53 percent want it decreased a little or a lot.
Turning to the top federal income tax rate, 37 percent of Californians believe it is too high vs. 15 percent who think it’s too low; nationally the figures are 37 percent vs. 20 percent. Again, contrary to the main media depiction of young adults, in California young adults are even more likely than their older fellow Californians to say the top federal income tax rate is too high (37–8 percent). While they may be frustrated at how expensive it is to buy a home in California, perhaps they retain the ambition to get ahead and see the top rate as a future problem that may well affect them. Nationally, the figures are a much closer 29–22 percent. Even the state Democrats say it is too high by 27–20 percent. Republicans, not surprisingly, are 55–5 for too high vs. too low. Independents are 37–15.
These results may in part reflect the fact that the federal personal income tax is not adjusted for geographic differences in the cost of living. So, people with the same nominal income in California as in, for example, Texas or Florida have a lower real income because of the higher cost of living. Hence, the top federal income tax rate starts to bite Californians at a lower “standard of living” than in almost all other states.
Interestingly, 51 percent of Californians believe the state personal income tax should be reduced a lot or a little, vs. 10 percent who want it increased a little and only 3 percent who want it increased a lot. Nationally, the figures are 53 percent who want their state income tax reduced while only 10 percent want it increased. In both surveys, the results are similar across race, age, and sex. California Democrats also want lower state income taxes (44–16), and Republicans (64–14) and independents (54–9) agree more strongly.
On the top state income tax rate, which in California is the highest in the nation, a plurality thinks it is about right and 28 percent think it is too low, vs. 24 percent who think it’s too high. Nationally, 49 percent believe their state income tax is about right but more think it is too high rather than too low, by 21 percent to 16 percent. Both Democrats (40–11 too low) and Republicans (42–9 too high) have stronger views than their national counterparts.
Interestingly, Californians favor cutting state property taxes, 47 percent to 15 percent, despite the allegations that the 1970s-era Proposition 13 property tax limitation has severely constrained property tax revenue. Nationally, the desire for lower state property taxes is even stronger: 62 percent favor cutting (of which 39 percent favor cutting a lot), while only 10 percent favor an increase. Likewise, Californians favor cutting the state’s sales tax, at 50 percent, vs. only 12 percent who want it increased; nationally, the figures are almost identical (50–9).
Lower taxes for other people? Not so much . . .
What Californians favor—or at least find less objectionable—are taxes they believe are paid by someone else. As the former powerful chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, Russell Long, quipped, “Tax reform means don’t tax you and don’t tax me, tax that fellow behind the tree.”
For example, by 45 percent to 22 percent, Californians favor raising the federal corporate tax; nationally the figures are almost identical: 45 percent to 23 percent. By 47 percent to 22 percent, Californians favor raising the state corporate tax; again, nationally the results are virtually identical: 44 percent vs. 23 percent. Interestingly, when asked the same question about state business taxes—the distinction between business and corporation taxes speaks to the difference between large companies and smaller unincorporated businesses—Californians are equally divided: 32 percent favoring an increase and the same number favoring a decrease. Nationally the numbers are similar: 32 percent increase, 29 percent decrease.
Economists—and official government scorekeepers, such as the Congressional Budget Office—warn that a sizable share of the business tax burden is shifted to workers in the form of lower wages than would otherwise be the case (and perhaps some also onto higher prices for consumers). This admonition appears not to have reached the general public. Nor has the fact that the corporate tax is paid by companies whose shares are held in almost all retirement savings accounts.
Finally, respondents both in California and nationally favor a generic wealth tax on the very rich.
How Prop 40 might break
This brings us to California’s Proposition 40, the so-called one-time wealth tax on billionaires. It seems perfectly suited to this view of taxing the rich, as it will directly apply to only 200 to 300 people. Its proponents undoubtedly designed it for popular appeal, while the UC-Berkeley economists giving it intellectual cover, Gabriel Zucman and Emmanuel Saez, call it “a start” and “an experiment,” respectively. Their arguments, which assume very little incentive to avoid or evade the tax, have been rebutted by the careful research of our Hoover colleagues Josh Rauh and Benjamin Jaros (https://www.wsj.com/opinion/california-prop-40-wealth-tax-revenue-loss-study-hoover-institution-4b533b72) . In fact, the tax is likely to cost the state revenue because of the decline in future income tax revenue from the flight of the wealthy, entrepreneurs, and jobs, and the dubious legality of its retroactive provision and other factors.
Paradoxically, while Proposition 40 is slightly ahead in most polls, it has struggled to get to the 50 percent threshold most political observers believe is necessary in polling for a proposition to prevail on the ballot. Why? Because historically, undecideds tend to break heavily against propositions that raise taxes.
In our polling, we disaggregate voters into six groups. We do this because of the structure of Propositions 40, 41 and 42. Proposition 41 would prohibit new taxes whose revenues are excempted from state spending limits approved by voters, and would require pre-approval and continuing audits. Proposition 42 prohibits new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement savings. Both are designed as potential safeguards against Prop 40 passing, because under California law if either 41 or 42 passes with a larger pro vote than Prop 40, Prop 40 would fail even if it had a majority in favor.
Our six groups are:
Those in favor of Prop 40 and opposed to or undecided on both 41 and 42, at 29 percent of likely voters.
Those who are negative or undecided on Prop 40 and not negative on the other two, at 30 percent of likely voters.
An additional 7 percent who are against all three and hence can be added to the anti–Prop 40 total.
An additional 18 percent who appear conflicted—that is, they are inconsistently yes on Prop 40 but also on at least one or the other of Props 41 and 42.
11 percent who are undecided on all three.
And the remaining 5 percent in an “other” category.

It thus appears the fate of the “billionaire wealth tax” will be decided by two primary factors: whether the undecideds break overwhelmingly against it, as is common on California ballot initiatives, and whether the apparently conflicted and/or confused voters overwhelmingly stay with their yes inclination.
Why the wealth tax is struggling
So why is Prop 40, explicitly designed to focus on “just a few” wealthy Californians, struggling to get to 50 percent? There are at least five reasons.
A voter drops off his ballot at a drive-through box last June in San Diego. [Michael Ho Wai Lee—SOPA Images-Sipa USA] First, the majority of Californians believe the state has a spending problem, not a tax problem, as described above. Californians also appear to have lost confidence in the state’s ability to manage its finances and its programs competently. By 56–14 percent, they do not believe that the money supposedly raised under the proposition is guaranteed to go as advertised to health care. Nor do they believe that hospitals and emergency rooms will close if it fails (36–27 percent). And, perhaps most distressing for those who believe in honesty and transparency in government, by 3 to 1 (48–16 percent), Californians say it is not believable that this is a one-time tax. Californians are evenly split (51–49) on whether the tax should be levied only when assets are sold.
Second, Californians are pessimistic about the ability to administer a wealth tax; 42 percent believe it’s a good idea in theory but impractical to administer, while 24 percent disagree. Nationally, the corresponding figures are tied at 34 percent each, perhaps because a national wealth tax may be thought easier to administer without capital flight than a state wealth tax. (Difficulty in administering wealth taxes and too little revenue raised are cited as the reasons most European countries, including Sweden and Denmark, which are often cited as desirable models by the progressive left, have abolished their wealth taxes.)
Digging deeper on administering the wealth tax envisioned in Prop 40, our polling data reveal a majority, 53 percent to 47 percent, believe the state will not be able to properly value the assets subject to the tax. The results differ markedly by age: the youngest two age cohorts—those with the least wealth and the least experience with it—are much more confident assets can be accurately valued (72–29 percent for 18- to 29-year-olds) than the oldest two age cohorts—those with much more wealth and experience managing it, who are not confident in accurate valuation (63–36 percent for those 65 and over).
Third, many Californians are confused about what the new tax in Prop 40 actually is and how it will work. Shockingly, barely a majority understand it applies to all assets. Remarkably, almost a quarter believe it is an additional income tax on 2026 income and just over a quarter are not sure. That raises the question of whether anything can be sound policy if almost half the population does not even know what it is.
Fourth, a resounding majority think billionaires will find a way to avoid paying the tax (67–6), with even higher shares among Democrats (72–6) and independents (69–2) than among Republicans (54–11). By large majorities, among all ages, races, sexes, and political affiliation groups, Californians believe it would be a serious problem if many of the state’s billionaires left the state.
Fifth, a host of concerns about deleterious incentive effects counterbalances the belief that billionaires aren’t paying their fair share (we did not ask a question to see if the respondents actually knew how much in taxes is paid by billionaires, although it is widely known in California that the top 1 percent income group pays 40-plus percent of the state income tax, which is the state’s major revenue source). A sizable majority believe a wealth tax would push startups and business expansion out of the state (40–27). Democrats disagree (25–40), while Republicans overwhelmingly (71–7) and independents decidedly (40–22) agree.
On the question of whether the Prop 40 wealth tax would raise or lower the state’s revenue, at the extremes, 10 percent believe it will raise a lot more, 17 percent a lot less; and “somewhat more” outpaces “somewhat less” by 2 to 1 (25–12). Interestingly, only a small percentage say it will raise about the same (around 12 percent). There are sharp differences by age: the youngest cohort believes it will raise more revenue (46–17, although mostly “somewhat more”); the oldest believes it will raise less (38–28).
Democrats believe it will raise more by 49–16 (although again, mostly “somewhat more,” not “a lot more”); Republicans believe the opposite by 55–19, but mostly “a lot less”; independents are about evenly split (33–29 more, although on the “more” side mostly “somewhat more” rather than “a lot more,” and on the “less” side mostly “a lot less” rather than “somewhat less”).
If Proposition 40 does indeed pass, its implementation may well be delayed by lawsuits contesting various provisions, from its retroactivity to its valuation methods to its proposed taxing of worldwide income and attempt to prohibit Congress from allowing a deduction for the tax against federal income taxes under the Commerce, Takings, and Due Process clauses of the U.S. Constitution. (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7554598)
Where attitudes meet policy
Whatever the outcome of the vote, the long-standing Democratic supermajority in Sacramento will continue, as will the likely control of all statewide offices from the governor on down. This means that only time will tell if our snapshot of Californians’ attitudes on taxes and spending will hold up over time and, more importantly, will actually, at some point, affect policy outcomes.

02 de noviembre de 2026

Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
SANTA FE SPRINGS, California, EU, 2 de noviembre de 2026.- AIMSA y Quadratín California presentaron los resultados de la Encuesta Electoral California 2026 realizada a dos mil personas, durante un encuentro celebrado en Casa AJUA, con la participación de líderes comunitarios y representantes del sector empresarial.
La presentación forma parte de una alianza entre ambas organizaciones para generar información sobre las preferencias electorales, las preocupaciones y la participación de los votantes, particularmente de la comunidad latina, mediante ejercicios de opinión pública que buscan tener continuidad en futuros procesos electorales.
Jesús Javier García Ruiz, director de AIMSA, explicó que el estudio permitió conocer con mayor detalle la composición del electorado hispano en California y comparar algunas tendencias con los resultados obtenidos previamente en San Diego.
Uno de los aspectos que destacó fue la participación del voto de origen mexicano, que representa aproximadamente una tercera parte del electorado hispano en el estado. “Es muy interesante que los hispanos pueden contribuir hacia elegir o a un candidato”, señaló García Ruiz.
Foto: Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
Al referirse a las preferencias electorales para la gubernatura, indicó que los resultados muestran una tendencia definida hacia el sector demócrata, con Xavier Becerra al frente (https://california.quadratin.com/politica/supera-xavier-becerra-por-25-puntos-a-steve-hilton-en-encuesta-de-aimsa/).
“Hay algunas iniciativas en donde la gente está interesada, sobre todo en el impuesto millonario, el tema de presentar una identificación para permitir la parte del voto, y hay otras que están muy cerradas y hoy están en fase técnica”, explicó.
El director de AIMSA agregó que el margen de error del estudio es de aproximadamente cinco puntos porcentuales, dependiendo del método utilizado para realizar las consultas, ya sea mediante mensajes SMS o llamadas telefónicas.
Foto: Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
Destacan potencial del voto latino
Durante el encuentro también participó Tayde Aburto, director y fundador de la Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce de San Diego , quien destacó el peso que puede tener la comunidad latina en los procesos electorales de California.
Aburto señaló que uno de los datos que más le llamó la atención fue que existen 8.2 millones de latinos con posibilidad de votar en el estado; sin embargo, manifestó preocupación por el nivel de participación de este sector.
“Es muy refrescante saber que somos una comunidad que podemos cambiar las tendencias en ciertas elecciones”, expresó.
Consideró necesario impulsar iniciativas y campañas que motiven a los latinos a ejercer su derecho al voto, especialmente porque las decisiones políticas pueden tener repercusiones en sus familias y negocios.
Foto: Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
Desde su experiencia en el sector empresarial, explicó que los propietarios de negocios suelen prestar mayor atención a las propuestas relacionadas con impuestos y políticas públicas, debido a sus posibles efectos en los costos de operación y la rentabilidad.
Asimismo, destacó la importancia de que los ciudadanos tengan acceso a información diversa y equilibrada para tomar decisiones propias.
“Tenemos que informarnos para que no votemos siempre en bloque”, afirmó Aburto, quien consideró que cada persona debe decidir de acuerdo con lo que considera mejor para su familia, su negocio y su comunidad.
El encuentro contó también con la participación de Leo Espinoza, presidente de Quadratín Hispano y Quadratín California, además de líderes comunitarios que acudieron a conocer los resultados y dialogar sobre la importancia de la participación ciudadana.
La alianza entre AIMSA y Quadratín busca dar continuidad a estos ejercicios de investigación y difusión para ofrecer información sobre las opiniones y preocupaciones de la comunidad latina y contribuir a una ciudadanía mejor informada.
Para consultar una reseña de los resultados de la encuesta, visita el reporte de Quadratín California : Aumenta voto anticipado entre encuestados en California (https://california.quadratin.com/politica/aumenta-voto-anticipado-entre-encuestados-en-california/).

Presentan AIMSA y Quadratín encuesta sobre el voto latino en California
02 de noviembre de 2026
,
17:13
Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
SANTA FE SPRINGS, California, EU, 2 de noviembre de 2026.- AIMSA y Quadratín California presentaron los resultados de la Encuesta Electoral California 2026 realizada a dos mil personas, durante un encuentro celebrado en Casa AJUA, con la participación de líderes comunitarios y representantes del sector empresarial.
La presentación forma parte de una alianza entre ambas organizaciones para generar información sobre las preferencias electorales, las preocupaciones y la participación de los votantes, particularmente de la comunidad latina, mediante ejercicios de opinión pública que buscan tener continuidad en futuros procesos electorales.
Jesús Javier García Ruiz, director de AIMSA, explicó que el estudio permitió conocer con mayor detalle la composición del electorado hispano en California y comparar algunas tendencias con los resultados obtenidos previamente en San Diego.
Uno de los aspectos que destacó fue la participación del voto de origen mexicano, que representa aproximadamente una tercera parte del electorado hispano en el estado. “Es muy interesante que los hispanos pueden contribuir hacia elegir o a un candidato”, señaló García Ruiz.
Foto: Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
Al referirse a las preferencias electorales para la gubernatura, indicó que los resultados muestran una tendencia definida hacia el sector demócrata, con Xavier Becerra al frente (https://california.quadratin.com/politica/supera-xavier-becerra-por-25-puntos-a-steve-hilton-en-encuesta-de-aimsa/).
“Hay algunas iniciativas en donde la gente está interesada, sobre todo en el impuesto millonario, el tema de presentar una identificación para permitir la parte del voto, y hay otras que están muy cerradas y hoy están en fase técnica”, explicó.
El director de AIMSA agregó que el margen de error del estudio es de aproximadamente cinco puntos porcentuales, dependiendo del método utilizado para realizar las consultas, ya sea mediante mensajes SMS o llamadas telefónicas.
Foto: Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
Destacan potencial del voto latino
Durante el encuentro también participó Tayde Aburto, director y fundador de la Hispanic Chamber of E-Commerce de San Diego , quien destacó el peso que puede tener la comunidad latina en los procesos electorales de California.
Aburto señaló que uno de los datos que más le llamó la atención fue que existen 8.2 millones de latinos con posibilidad de votar en el estado; sin embargo, manifestó preocupación por el nivel de participación de este sector.
“Es muy refrescante saber que somos una comunidad que podemos cambiar las tendencias en ciertas elecciones”, expresó.
Consideró necesario impulsar iniciativas y campañas que motiven a los latinos a ejercer su derecho al voto, especialmente porque las decisiones políticas pueden tener repercusiones en sus familias y negocios.
Foto: Emma Mejía/Quadratín California
Desde su experiencia en el sector empresarial, explicó que los propietarios de negocios suelen prestar mayor atención a las propuestas relacionadas con impuestos y políticas públicas, debido a sus posibles efectos en los costos de operación y la rentabilidad.
Asimismo, destacó la importancia de que los ciudadanos tengan acceso a información diversa y equilibrada para tomar decisiones propias.
“Tenemos que informarnos para que no votemos siempre en bloque”, afirmó Aburto, quien consideró que cada persona debe decidir de acuerdo con lo que considera mejor para su familia, su negocio y su comunidad.
El encuentro contó también con la participación de Leo Espinoza, presidente de Quadratín Hispano y Quadratín California, además de líderes comunitarios que acudieron a conocer los resultados y dialogar sobre la importancia de la participación ciudadana.
La alianza entre AIMSA y Quadratín busca dar continuidad a estos ejercicios de investigación y difusión para ofrecer información sobre las opiniones y preocupaciones de la comunidad latina y contribuir a una ciudadanía mejor informada.
Para consultar una reseña de los resultados de la encuesta, visita el reporte de Quadratín California : Aumenta voto anticipado entre encuestados en California (https://california.quadratin.com/politica/aumenta-voto-anticipado-entre-encuestados-en-california/).

What Californians Really Want
As Election Day nears, voters aren’t clamoring for higher taxes or spending. A new poll shows surprising overlap with others across America.
By Michael J. Boskin (https://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/a/michael-j-boskin) and Douglas Rivers (https://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/a/douglas-rivers)
Thursday, October 29, 2026
23 3 Share
With the debates surrounding the proposed taxes on California’s November 3 ballot and the characterization of California as a high-tax, high-spending, heavy-welfare state, it may seem surprising that this is not what Californians really want.
JOIN THE COMMUNITY (http://www.thefreedomfrequency.org/subscribe)
In fact, Californians’ views on taxes and spending are quite similar to the views of the rest of the country in many dimensions. A careful look at their attitudes towards taxes and spending is necessary, so this month YouGov conducted parallel national and California surveys for us focused precisely on these issues.
Californians aren’t that different
Before turning to taxes, here is some of the evidence that California and the rest of the country are quite similar in how they feel about the future.
Optimism: Californians are 45 percent very or somewhat optimistic, versus 34 percent who are somewhat or very pessimistic. The corresponding figures nationally are 44 percent versus 35 percent. Contrary to conventional media narratives, young adults are the most optimistic, both nationally (48 to 32 percent) and in California (53 to 28 percent). The state’s Democrats are equally divided, as are independents, while Republicans, who comprise just a quarter of California’s registered voters, are overwhelmingly optimistic (67–16 percent). Perhaps this is because they support many of the policies pursued nationally by the Trump administration, which more than offsets their dissatisfaction with state policy.
What kind of economy? When asked about their preferred economic system, 15 percent of Californians say they prefer socialism and 2 percent communism, versus 16 percent and 2 percent nationally. There is a modest difference in that 42 percent of Californians prefer a mixed capitalist/socialist model versus 35 percent nationally, whereas nationally 35 percent prefer a pure capitalist model versus only 25 percent in California.
A “vote” poster combines with a Grateful Dead symbol at a Democratic Party rally Oct. 23 in San Francisco. [Heather Diehl—Associated Press] Interestingly, while no sex, race, or age group favors socialism by more than 17 percent, black Californians favor capitalism least and overwhelmingly favor a mixed capitalist-socialist model, whereas Asians are the least favorable to socialism at 9 percent. While the majority of Democrats in the state favor a mixed system (54 percent), they favor socialism to capitalism by 3 to 1, whereas Republicans overwhelmingly favor capitalism (64 percent to 4 percent for socialism), with independents favoring capitalism by 2 to 1 over socialism (28–13 percent), but a plurality favors a mixed system (43 percent). We prefaced these questions with a series that gave various definitions and features of capitalism and socialism, so the possibility that different groups have different ideas about the nature of each of these systems is somewhat mitigated. At the national level, the results are similar. Notable differences include middle-aged and older respondents being even more favorable to capitalism over a mixed model than in California.
A spending problem : Of those agreeing or disagreeing, Californians are even more in agreement that their state has a spending problem, not a revenue problem, by 48 percent to 20 percent, whereas nationally the figures are 43 percent vs. 19 percent. In both cases, the pattern holds across all ages, but is even more pronounced for older respondents, still more so in California.
Anti-business: One area where California differs is that slightly more Californians think their state is more anti-business than pro-business, with sharp differences by age: the two youngest groups think the state is more pro-business and the two older groups, more anti-business. Politically, Democrats believe the state is more pro-business by 37–14 percent, Republicans lean the other way, more strongly, at 15–56 percent, with independents leaning anti- by 12 points. Nationally, the picture is dramatically different: 41 percent believe their state is pro-business vs. only 15 percent anti-business.
Californians want lower taxes for themselves
It turns out Californians really don’t like high taxes, including high tax rates, especially (unsurprisingly) when they believe they may wind up paying them now or in the future.
Californians believe the federal personal income tax should be reduced: 47 percent want it decreased vs. 16 percent who want it increased (26 percent want it kept the same and 12 percent are unsure). Nationally, the views are even more lopsided: 14 percent would like it increased, 53 percent want it decreased a little or a lot.
Turning to the top federal income tax rate, 37 percent of Californians believe it is too high vs. 15 percent who think it’s too low; nationally the figures are 37 percent vs. 20 percent. Again, contrary to the main media depiction of young adults, in California young adults are even more likely than their older fellow Californians to say the top federal income tax rate is too high (37–8 percent). While they may be frustrated at how expensive it is to buy a home in California, perhaps they retain the ambition to get ahead and see the top rate as a future problem that may well affect them. Nationally, the figures are a much closer 29–22 percent. Even the state Democrats say it is too high by 27–20 percent. Republicans, not surprisingly, are 55–5 for too high vs. too low. Independents are 37–15.
These results may in part reflect the fact that the federal personal income tax is not adjusted for geographic differences in the cost of living. So, people with the same nominal income in California as in, for example, Texas or Florida have a lower real income because of the higher cost of living. Hence, the top federal income tax rate starts to bite Californians at a lower “standard of living” than in almost all other states.
Interestingly, 51 percent of Californians believe the state personal income tax should be reduced a lot or a little, vs. 10 percent who want it increased a little and only 3 percent who want it increased a lot. Nationally, the figures are 53 percent who want their state income tax reduced while only 10 percent want it increased. In both surveys, the results are similar across race, age, and sex. California Democrats also want lower state income taxes (44–16), and Republicans (64–14) and independents (54–9) agree more strongly.
On the top state income tax rate, which in California is the highest in the nation, a plurality thinks it is about right and 28 percent think it is too low, vs. 24 percent who think it’s too high. Nationally, 49 percent believe their state income tax is about right but more think it is too high rather than too low, by 21 percent to 16 percent. Both Democrats (40–11 too low) and Republicans (42–9 too high) have stronger views than their national counterparts.
Interestingly, Californians favor cutting state property taxes, 47 percent to 15 percent, despite the allegations that the 1970s-era Proposition 13 property tax limitation has severely constrained property tax revenue. Nationally, the desire for lower state property taxes is even stronger: 62 percent favor cutting (of which 39 percent favor cutting a lot), while only 10 percent favor an increase. Likewise, Californians favor cutting the state’s sales tax, at 50 percent, vs. only 12 percent who want it increased; nationally, the figures are almost identical (50–9).
Lower taxes for other people? Not so much . . .
What Californians favor—or at least find less objectionable—are taxes they believe are paid by someone else. As the former powerful chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, Russell Long, quipped, “Tax reform means don’t tax you and don’t tax me, tax that fellow behind the tree.”
For example, by 45 percent to 22 percent, Californians favor raising the federal corporate tax; nationally the figures are almost identical: 45 percent to 23 percent. By 47 percent to 22 percent, Californians favor raising the state corporate tax; again, nationally the results are virtually identical: 44 percent vs. 23 percent. Interestingly, when asked the same question about state business taxes—the distinction between business and corporation taxes speaks to the difference between large companies and smaller unincorporated businesses—Californians are equally divided: 32 percent favoring an increase and the same number favoring a decrease. Nationally the numbers are similar: 32 percent increase, 29 percent decrease.
Economists—and official government scorekeepers, such as the Congressional Budget Office—warn that a sizable share of the business tax burden is shifted to workers in the form of lower wages than would otherwise be the case (and perhaps some also onto higher prices for consumers). This admonition appears not to have reached the general public. Nor has the fact that the corporate tax is paid by companies whose shares are held in almost all retirement savings accounts.
Finally, respondents both in California and nationally favor a generic wealth tax on the very rich.
How Prop 40 might break
This brings us to California’s Proposition 40, the so-called one-time wealth tax on billionaires. It seems perfectly suited to this view of taxing the rich, as it will directly apply to only 200 to 300 people. Its proponents undoubtedly designed it for popular appeal, while the UC-Berkeley economists giving it intellectual cover, Gabriel Zucman and Emmanuel Saez, call it “a start” and “an experiment,” respectively. Their arguments, which assume very little incentive to avoid or evade the tax, have been rebutted by the careful research of our Hoover colleagues Josh Rauh and Benjamin Jaros (https://www.wsj.com/opinion/california-prop-40-wealth-tax-revenue-loss-study-hoover-institution-4b533b72) . In fact, the tax is likely to cost the state revenue because of the decline in future income tax revenue from the flight of the wealthy, entrepreneurs, and jobs, and the dubious legality of its retroactive provision and other factors.
Paradoxically, while Proposition 40 is slightly ahead in most polls, it has struggled to get to the 50 percent threshold most political observers believe is necessary in polling for a proposition to prevail on the ballot. Why? Because historically, undecideds tend to break heavily against propositions that raise taxes.
In our polling, we disaggregate voters into six groups. We do this because of the structure of Propositions 40, 41 and 42. Proposition 41 would prohibit new taxes whose revenues are excempted from state spending limits approved by voters, and would require pre-approval and continuing audits. Proposition 42 prohibits new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement savings. Both are designed as potential safeguards against Prop 40 passing, because under California law if either 41 or 42 passes with a larger pro vote than Prop 40, Prop 40 would fail even if it had a majority in favor.
Our six groups are:
Those in favor of Prop 40 and opposed to or undecided on both 41 and 42, at 29 percent of likely voters.
Those who are negative or undecided on Prop 40 and not negative on the other two, at 30 percent of likely voters.
An additional 7 percent who are against all three and hence can be added to the anti–Prop 40 total.
An additional 18 percent who appear conflicted—that is, they are inconsistently yes on Prop 40 but also on at least one or the other of Props 41 and 42.
11 percent who are undecided on all three.
And the remaining 5 percent in an “other” category.
The following table presents these numbers.
It thus appears the fate of the “billionaire wealth tax” will be decided by two primary factors: whether the undecideds break overwhelmingly against it, as is common on California ballot initiatives, and whether the apparently conflicted and/or confused voters overwhelmingly stay with their yes inclination.
Why the wealth tax is struggling
So why is Prop 40, explicitly designed to focus on “just a few” wealthy Californians, struggling to get to 50 percent? There are at least five reasons.
A voter drops off his ballot at a drive-through box last June in San Diego. [Michael Ho Wai Lee—SOPA Images-Sipa USA] First, the majority of Californians believe the state has a spending problem, not a tax problem, as described above. Californians also appear to have lost confidence in the state’s ability to manage its finances and its programs competently. By 56–14 percent, they do not believe that the money supposedly raised under the proposition is guaranteed to go as advertised to health care. Nor do they believe that hospitals and emergency rooms will close if it fails (36–27 percent). And, perhaps most distressing for those who believe in honesty and transparency in government, by 3 to 1 (48–16 percent), Californians say it is not believable that this is a one-time tax. Californians are evenly split (51–49) on whether the tax should be levied only when assets are sold.
Second, Californians are pessimistic about the ability to administer a wealth tax; 42 percent believe it’s a good idea in theory but impractical to administer, while 24 percent disagree. Nationally, the corresponding figures are tied at 34 percent each, perhaps because a national wealth tax may be thought easier to administer without capital flight than a state wealth tax. (Difficulty in administering wealth taxes and too little revenue raised are cited as the reasons most European countries, including Sweden and Denmark, which are often cited as desirable models by the progressive left, have abolished their wealth taxes.)
Digging deeper on administering the wealth tax envisioned in Prop 40, our polling data reveal a majority, 53 percent to 47 percent, believe the state will not be able to properly value the assets subject to the tax. The results differ markedly by age: the youngest two age cohorts—those with the least wealth and the least experience with it—are much more confident assets can be accurately valued (72–29 percent for 18- to 29-year-olds) than the oldest two age cohorts—those with much more wealth and experience managing it, who are not confident in accurate valuation (63–36 percent for those 65 and over).
Third, many Californians are confused about what the new tax in Prop 40 actually is and how it will work. Shockingly, barely a majority understand it applies to all assets. Remarkably, almost a quarter believe it is an additional income tax on 2026 income and just over a quarter are not sure. That raises the question of whether anything can be sound policy if almost half the population does not even know what it is.
Fourth, a resounding majority think billionaires will find a way to avoid paying the tax (67–6), with even higher shares among Democrats (72–6) and independents (69–2) than among Republicans (54–11). By large majorities, among all ages, races, sexes, and political affiliation groups, Californians believe it would be a serious problem if many of the state’s billionaires left the state.
Fifth, a host of concerns about deleterious incentive effects counterbalances the belief that billionaires aren’t paying their fair share (we did not ask a question to see if the respondents actually knew how much in taxes is paid by billionaires, although it is widely known in California that the top 1 percent income group pays 40-plus percent of the state income tax, which is the state’s major revenue source). A sizable majority believe a wealth tax would push startups and business expansion out of the state (40–27). Democrats disagree (25–40), while Republicans overwhelmingly (71–7) and independents decidedly (40–22) agree.
On the question of whether the Prop 40 wealth tax would raise or lower the state’s revenue, at the extremes, 10 percent believe it will raise a lot more, 17 percent a lot less; and “somewhat more” outpaces “somewhat less” by 2 to 1 (25–12). Interestingly, only a small percentage say it will raise about the same (around 12 percent). There are sharp differences by age: the youngest cohort believes it will raise more revenue (46–17, although mostly “somewhat more”); the oldest believes it will raise less (38–28).
Democrats believe it will raise more by 49–16 (although again, mostly “somewhat more,” not “a lot more”); Republicans believe the opposite by 55–19, but mostly “a lot less”; independents are about evenly split (33–29 more, although on the “more” side mostly “somewhat more” rather than “a lot more,” and on the “less” side mostly “a lot less” rather than “somewhat less”).
If Proposition 40 does indeed pass, its implementation may well be delayed by lawsuits contesting various provisions, from its retroactivity to its valuation methods to its proposed taxing of worldwide income and attempt to prohibit Congress from allowing a deduction for the tax against federal income taxes under the Commerce, Takings, and Due Process clauses of the U.S. Constitution. (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7554598)
Where attitudes meet policy
Whatever the outcome of the vote, the long-standing Democratic supermajority in Sacramento will continue, as will the likely control of all statewide offices from the governor on down. This means that only time will tell if our snapshot of Californians’ attitudes on taxes and spending will hold up over time and, more importantly, will actually, at some point, affect policy outcomes.

On the top state income tax rate, which in California is the highest in the nation, a plurality thinks it is about right and 28 percent think it is too low, vs. 24 percent who think it’s too high. Nationally, 49 percent believe their state income tax is about right but more think it is too high rather than too low, by 21 percent to 16 percent. Both Democrats (40–11 too low) and Republicans (42–9 too high) have stronger views than their national counterparts.
Interestingly, Californians favor cutting state property taxes, 47 percent to 15 percent, despite the allegations that the 1970s-era Proposition 13 property tax limitation has severely constrained property tax revenue. Nationally, the desire for lower state property taxes is even stronger: 62 percent favor cutting (of which 39 percent favor cutting a lot), while only 10 percent favor an increase. Likewise, Californians favor cutting the state’s sales tax, at 50 percent, vs. only 12 percent who want it increased; nationally, the figures are almost identical (50–9).
Lower taxes for other people? Not so much . . .
What Californians favor—or at least find less objectionable—are taxes they believe are paid by someone else. As the former powerful chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, Russell Long, quipped, “Tax reform means don’t tax you and don’t tax me, tax that fellow behind the tree.”
For example, by 45 percent to 22 percent, Californians favor raising the federal corporate tax; nationally the figures are almost identical: 45 percent to 23 percent. By 47 percent to 22 percent, Californians favor raising the state corporate tax; again, nationally the results are virtually identical: 44 percent vs. 23 percent. Interestingly, when asked the same question about state business taxes—the distinction between business and corporation taxes speaks to the difference between large companies and smaller unincorporated businesses—Californians are equally divided: 32 percent favoring an increase and the same number favoring a decrease. Nationally the numbers are similar: 32 percent increase, 29 percent decrease.
Economists—and official government scorekeepers, such as the Congressional Budget Office—warn that a sizable share of the business tax burden is shifted to workers in the form of lower wages than would otherwise be the case (and perhaps some also onto higher prices for consumers). This admonition appears not to have reached the general public. Nor has the fact that the corporate tax is paid by companies whose shares are held in almost all retirement savings accounts.
Finally, respondents both in California and nationally favor a generic wealth tax on the very rich.
How Prop 40 might break
This brings us to California’s Proposition 40, the so-called one-time wealth tax on billionaires. It seems perfectly suited to this view of taxing the rich, as it will directly apply to only 200 to 300 people. Its proponents undoubtedly designed it for popular appeal, while the UC-Berkeley economists giving it intellectual cover, Gabriel Zucman and Emmanuel Saez, call it “a start” and “an experiment,” respectively. Their arguments, which assume very little incentive to avoid or evade the tax, have been rebutted by the careful research of our Hoover colleagues Josh Rauh and Benjamin Jaros (https://www.wsj.com/opinion/california-prop-40-wealth-tax-revenue-loss-study-hoover-institution-4b533b72) . In fact, the tax is likely to cost the state revenue because of the decline in future income tax revenue from the flight of the wealthy, entrepreneurs, and jobs, and the dubious legality of its retroactive provision and other factors.
Paradoxically, while Proposition 40 is slightly ahead in most polls, it has struggled to get to the 50 percent threshold most political observers believe is necessary in polling for a proposition to prevail on the ballot. Why? Because historically, undecideds tend to break heavily against propositions that raise taxes.
In our polling, we disaggregate voters into six groups. We do this because of the structure of Propositions 40, 41 and 42. Proposition 41 would prohibit new taxes whose revenues are excempted from state spending limits approved by voters, and would require pre-approval and continuing audits. Proposition 42 prohibits new and retroactive taxes on personal property, including retirement savings. Both are designed as potential safeguards against Prop 40 passing, because under California law if either 41 or 42 passes with a larger pro vote than Prop 40, Prop 40 would fail even if it had a majority in favor.
Our six groups are:
Those in favor of Prop 40 and opposed to or undecided on both 41 and 42, at 29 percent of likely voters.
Those who are negative or undecided on Prop 40 and not negative on the other two, at 30 percent of likely voters.
An additional 7 percent who are against all three and hence can be added to the anti–Prop 40 total.
An additional 18 percent who appear conflicted—that is, they are inconsistently yes on Prop 40 but also on at least one or the other of Props 41 and 42.
11 percent who are undecided on all three.
And the remaining 5 percent in an “other” category.
The following table presents these numbers.
It thus appears the fate of the “billionaire wealth tax” will be decided by two primary factors: whether the undecideds break overwhelmingly against it, as is common on California ballot initiatives, and whether the apparently conflicted and/or confused voters overwhelmingly stay with their yes inclination.
Why the wealth tax is struggling
So why is Prop 40, explicitly designed to focus on “just a few” wealthy Californians, struggling to get to 50 percent? There are at least five reasons.
A voter drops off his ballot at a drive-through box last June in San Diego. [Michael Ho Wai Lee—SOPA Images-Sipa USA] First, the majority of Californians believe the state has a spending problem, not a tax problem, as described above. Californians also appear to have lost confidence in the state’s ability to manage its finances and its programs competently. By 56–14 percent, they do not believe that the money supposedly raised under the proposition is guaranteed to go as advertised to health care. Nor do they believe that hospitals and emergency rooms will close if it fails (36–27 percent). And, perhaps most distressing for those who believe in honesty and transparency in government, by 3 to 1 (48–16 percent), Californians say it is not believable that this is a one-time tax. Californians are evenly split (51–49) on whether the tax should be levied only when assets are sold.
Second, Californians are pessimistic about the ability to administer a wealth tax; 42 percent believe it’s a good idea in theory but impractical to administer, while 24 percent disagree. Nationally, the corresponding figures are tied at 34 percent each, perhaps because a national wealth tax may be thought easier to administer without capital flight than a state wealth tax. (Difficulty in administering wealth taxes and too little revenue raised are cited as the reasons most European countries, including Sweden and Denmark, which are often cited as desirable models by the progressive left, have abolished their wealth taxes.)
Digging deeper on administering the wealth tax envisioned in Prop 40, our polling data reveal a majority, 53 percent to 47 percent, believe the state will not be able to properly value the assets subject to the tax. The results differ markedly by age: the youngest two age cohorts—those with the least wealth and the least experience with it—are much more confident assets can be accurately valued (72–29 percent for 18- to 29-year-olds) than the oldest two age cohorts—those with much more wealth and experience managing it, who are not confident in accurate valuation (63–36 percent for those 65 and over).
Third, many Californians are confused about what the new tax in Prop 40 actually is and how it will work. Shockingly, barely a majority understand it applies to all assets. Remarkably, almost a quarter believe it is an additional income tax on 2026 income and just over a quarter are not sure. That raises the question of whether anything can be sound policy if almost half the population does not even know what it is.
Fourth, a resounding majority think billionaires will find a way to avoid paying the tax (67–6), with even higher shares among Democrats (72–6) and independents (69–2) than among Republicans (54–11). By large majorities, among all ages, races, sexes, and political affiliation groups, Californians believe it would be a serious problem if many of the state’s billionaires left the state.
Fifth, a host of concerns about deleterious incentive effects counterbalances the belief that billionaires aren’t paying their fair share (we did not ask a question to see if the respondents actually knew how much in taxes is paid by billionaires, although it is widely known in California that the top 1 percent income group pays 40-plus percent of the state income tax, which is the state’s major revenue source). A sizable majority believe a wealth tax would push startups and business expansion out of the state (40–27). Democrats disagree (25–40), while Republicans overwhelmingly (71–7) and independents decidedly (40–22) agree.
On the question of whether the Prop 40 wealth tax would raise or lower the state’s revenue, at the extremes, 10 percent believe it will raise a lot more, 17 percent a lot less; and “somewhat more” outpaces “somewhat less” by 2 to 1 (25–12). Interestingly, only a small percentage say it will raise about the same (around 12 percent). There are sharp differences by age: the youngest cohort believes it will raise more revenue (46–17, although mostly “somewhat more”); the oldest believes it will raise less (38–28).
Democrats believe it will raise more by 49–16 (although again, mostly “somewhat more,” not “a lot more”); Republicans believe the opposite by 55–19, but mostly “a lot less”; independents are about evenly split (33–29 more, although on the “more” side mostly “somewhat more” rather than “a lot more,” and on the “less” side mostly “a lot less” rather than “somewhat less”).
If Proposition 40 does indeed pass, its implementation may well be delayed by lawsuits contesting various provisions, from its retroactivity to its valuation methods to its proposed taxing of worldwide income and attempt to prohibit Congress from allowing a deduction for the tax against federal income taxes under the Commerce, Takings, and Due Process clauses of the U.S. Constitution. (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7554598)
Where attitudes meet policy
Whatever the outcome of the vote, the long-standing Democratic supermajority in Sacramento will continue, as will the likely control of all statewide offices from the governor on down. This means that only time will tell if our snapshot of Californians’ attitudes on taxes and spending will hold up over time and, more importantly, will actually, at some point, affect policy outcomes.
